docs.text: Name What it does Example DNSSECIETF (RFC 4033-4035) · Standard · Recommended Adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can detect forged answers; trust chains up to the signed root zone. US federal .gov domains must be DNSSEC-signed, so validating resolvers reject a forged answer pointing a government site elsewhere. DNS over HTTPS (DoH)IETF (RFC 8484) · Protocol · Recommended Sends DNS lookups inside encrypted HTTPS so networks cannot see or tamper with the names you look up. Firefox uses DoH by default for US users, and Windows 11 can encrypt DNS for every app on the PC. DNS over TLS (DoT)IETF (RFC 7858) · Protocol · Recommended Encrypts DNS inside a dedicated TLS connection on port 853. Android's 'Private DNS' setting sends lookups over DoT to resolvers such as Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's dns.google. Oblivious DNS over HTTPS (ODoH)IETF (RFC 9230); Cloudflare, Apple · Protocol · Emerging A proxy hides your IP address from the DNS resolver, while encryption hides your query from the proxy, so no single party sees both. iCloud Private Relay uses oblivious DNS, so neither Apple nor the DNS provider learns both who you are and which sites you look up. RPKI for BGPIETF / Regional Internet Registries · Standard · Recommended Signed records (ROAs) state which network may announce which IP addresses, so routers can drop invalid routes. Large networks such as Cloudflare and AT&T filter RPKI-invalid routes, limiting accidental leaks and deliberate route hijacks. ASPA (route-leak protection)IETF SIDROPS drafts; Regional Internet Registries · Standard · Emerging Autonomous System Provider Authorization: signed RPKI records listing a network's upstream providers, so routers can spot route leaks that origin checks miss. A small ISP publishes ASPA naming its two transit providers, so a customer accidentally re-announcing its routes elsewhere is flagged as a leak. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)IETF (RFC 9849, 2026) · Protocol · Emerging Encrypts the website name inside the TLS handshake, which networks could previously read in plain text. Cloudflare enables ECH for its sites, Chrome and Firefox support it and OpenSSL 4.0 added it, hiding which site you visit from Wi-Fi snoops. NTS (Network Time Security)IETF (RFC 8915) · Protocol · Recommended Authenticates time from internet clocks so attackers cannot feed false times that break certificates and logs. Cloudflare and Netnod run public NTS servers, and Linux's chrony time service can use them with one config line. DANE (TLSA)IETF (RFC 6698, RFC 7672) · Standard · Acceptable Publishes a server's certificate details in DNSSEC-signed DNS; mainly used to enforce encryption between mail servers. Several mail providers, including Microsoft Exchange Online, support DANE for SMTP to stop attackers stripping email encryption. DKIM (with SPF and DMARC)IETF (RFC 6376) · Standard · Recommended Mail servers sign outgoing email; receivers verify using a public key in DNS, helping block spoofed senders. Gmail and Yahoo (2024) and Outlook.com (2025) require bulk senders to use DKIM, SPF and DMARC, cutting spoofed 'from your bank' emails.

docs.title: 9.13 Blockchain & Cryptocurrency
docs.text:
Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum are built almost entirely from cryptography: hashes chain blocks together so history cannot be quietly rewritten, and digital signatures prove only a wallet's owner can spend its coins. There is no bank to call: whoever holds the private key controls the funds.

From recovery words to a confirmed payment. Everything rests on the private key: whoever holds the recovery words controls the funds, and no one can reverse a confirmed payment.

Think of it like…

A blockchain is like a shared notebook copied to thousands of people, where each page is glued to the previous one with a seal that breaks if anyone edits an old page.

Real-world example

Mia buys a hardware wallet and writes its 24 recovery words on paper. When she sends Bitcoin to a friend, the wallet signs the transaction with her private key inside the device; computers worldwide check the signature, and miners add it to a block secured by SHA-256 proof of work. Her friend's exchange uses an MPC wallet, so no single server or employee ever holds a complete key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A wallet creates a private key from random recovery words.
  2. The public address is derived from the public key using hashing.
  3. To spend, the wallet signs the transaction with the private key.
  4. Network nodes verify signatures; Merkle trees summarise all transactions in each block.
  5. Proof of work or proof of stake decides who adds the next block.

Who uses it

Crypto exchanges, wallet makers, custodians, fintechs, central-bank researchers and individual investors.

Key takeaway

Keep recovery phrases offline, use hardware, multisig or MPC wallets for large sums, and remember that lost keys mean lost funds.

Going deeper

  • Bitcoin adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to keep blocks about 10 minutes apart; merchants commonly wait around six confirmations, roughly an hour, for large payments.
  • Ethereum's switch from proof of work to proof of stake in September 2022 cut its energy use by more than 99.9%, replacing hashing races with BLS-signed validator votes.
  • Smart contracts are code that holds money: audits, formal verification and bug bounties matter because a deployed contract usually cannot be patched.
  • Most large losses are key-management and interface failures, not broken maths: exchange hot-wallet compromises, phished recovery phrases, malicious contracts and 'blind signing'.
  • Shor's algorithm on a large quantum computer would break secp256k1 and Ed25519; coins whose public keys are already on-chain are most exposed, and Bitcoin developers are debating post-quantum address types.
  • Business custody combines multisig or MPC signing, hardware-isolated keys, withdrawal allowlists, time delays and independent verification of every transaction on a separate device.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Storing recovery words in a photo, cloud note or email; anyone who sees them owns the wallet.
  • Blind signing: approving a transaction the device screen cannot fully display; verify address and amount on trusted hardware.
  • Believing blockchain payments are anonymous: they are public forever and often linked to real identities through exchanges.
  • Typing a recovery phrase into a website or 'support' chat; legitimate wallets and exchanges never ask for it.

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example SHA-256 proof of workBitcoin (Satoshi Nakamoto) · Technique · Acceptable Miners repeatedly hash block headers with double SHA-256 until the result is below a target, making history costly to rewrite. Rewriting a confirmed Bitcoin payment would need more hashing power than the rest of the global network combined. Ethereum proof of stakeEthereum (since the September 2022 Merge) · Consensus · Recommended Validators who stake 32 ETH propose and vote on blocks with BLS signatures; provably signing conflicting blocks is punished by 'slashing' their stake. A staking provider runs validator keys in remote signers with slashing protection, because signing two conflicting blocks would destroy part of its customers' deposits. Bitcoin & Ethereum transaction signatures (ECDSA)Bitcoin, Ethereum; secp256k1 curve (SECG) · Technique · Acceptable Wallets sign each transaction with ECDSA on the secp256k1 curve; every node checks the signature against the sender's public key before accepting it. A 2013 Android random-number bug let thieves recover keys from weak Bitcoin signatures, so modern wallets derive signing nonces deterministically (RFC 6979). Taproot (BIP-341)Bitcoin (BIP-340, BIP-341, BIP-342) · Protocol upgrade · Recommended Bitcoin's 2021 upgrade adding Schnorr signatures and script trees, so complex spending rules stay hidden unless they are actually used. A company's shared Taproot wallet can spend in a way that looks like an ordinary single-signer payment on the blockchain. Wallet addresses & checksumsBitcoin (Base58Check, Bech32/Bech32m); Ethereum (EIP-55) · Technique · Recommended Addresses are hashes of public keys encoded with built-in checksums that catch typing mistakes before money is sent. Pasting a bc1 address with one wrong character fails the Bech32 checksum, so the wallet refuses to send rather than losing the funds. Merkle treesRalph Merkle · Technique · Recommended A tree of hashes summarising many transactions in one 'root'; proves one item is included without downloading everything. A phone wallet confirms a payment is in a Bitcoin block with a short Merkle proof instead of downloading the whole block. HD wallets (BIP-32 / BIP-39)Bitcoin Improvement Proposals · Standard · Recommended BIP-39 turns randomness into 12-24 recovery words; BIP-32 derives an unlimited tree of keys from that one seed. Mia restores every account on a new device by typing her 24 words; anyone else who finds the words can do the same. Shamir backup (SLIP-39)SatoshiLabs (Trezor) · Standard · Recommended Splits a wallet's recovery secret into several word-list shares, any agreed number of which (for example 2 of 3) restores it. A family keeps three shares in different homes; a burglar finding one learns nothing, and losing one share does not lose the savings. MultisigBitcoin script; Safe on Ethereum · Technique · Recommended Requires several keys (for example 2 of 3) to approve a transaction, removing a single point of failure. A treasury needs 3 of 5 signers; the 2025 Bybit hack showed signers must verify exactly what their screens ask them to approve. Smart-contract wallets (ERC-4337)Ethereum community (ERC-4337, live since 2023) · Standard · Emerging Account abstraction turns wallets into smart contracts that can require passkeys, spending limits, multiple approvers or social recovery. A wallet app lets users approve payments with a phone passkey and regain access through trusted friends instead of a 24-word phrase. Lightning NetworkLightning developers (BOLT specifications) · Protocol · Acceptable Bitcoin payment channels: two parties lock funds in a 2-of-2 multisig and update balances off-chain; hash time-locked contracts route payments across channels. A café accepts small bitcoin payments over Lightning that settle in seconds with tiny fees; only channel openings and closings reach the blockchain.

docs.title: 9.14 Privacy-Enhancing & Advanced Cryptography
docs.text:
New kinds of cryptography let organisations use data without actually seeing it: calculate on encrypted numbers, prove facts without revealing details, or compare lists without sharing them. These 'privacy-enhancing technologies' are moving out of research papers and into phones, browsers and clouds.

Privacy-enhancing technologies at a glance

What stays hidden Real deployment Main cost Homomorphic encryption Data from the server Apple Live Caller ID Lookup Heavy compute, big ciphertexts Multi-party computation Each party's input Pay-gap studies, custody Many network rounds Zero-knowledge proofs Facts behind a claim Age checks, zk-rollups Slow proof generation Private set intersection Items not in common Breached-password checks Only answers set questions Confidential computing Data in use from cloud staff Apple Private Cloud Compute Trust in chip vendor Oblivious HTTP Who asked what Safe Browsing lookups Needs non-colluding relay Differential privacy Any one person in statistics 2020 US Census Noise reduces accuracy

Each technique hides something different and has its own cost; pick the cheapest one that meets the privacy goal.

Think of it like…

It is like a sealed glove box in a laboratory: workers can handle and process what is inside without ever touching it or seeing it directly.

Real-world example

Chloe's password manager warns that one of her passwords appeared in a breach; it checked against billions of leaked passwords without ever sending hers in readable form. An online wine shop confirms she is over 18 using a zero-knowledge proof, learning nothing about her birthday. Meanwhile two fictional hospitals study a rare disease together with secure multi-party computation, never exchanging raw patient records.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick the privacy goal: hide the data, hide the question, or hide who is asking.
  2. Encrypt or blind the input on the user's device.
  3. The server computes, compares or verifies without seeing the raw data.
  4. Only the final answer is revealed, and only to the right party.
  5. Independent audits and transparency logs confirm the system behaves as promised.

Who uses it

Big-tech privacy teams, healthcare and research consortia, advertising, banks fighting fraud and blockchain projects.

Key takeaway

These techniques are powerful but intricate: rely on mature libraries and audited services rather than custom designs.

Going deeper

  • Homomorphic schemes differ: BFV and BGV compute exactly on integers, CKKS works on approximate real numbers for machine learning, and TFHE evaluates bit-level logic quickly; all are lattice-based.
  • zk-SNARKs give tiny proofs but often need a trusted setup ceremony; zk-STARKs avoid trusted setup and rely only on hash functions, at the cost of larger proofs.
  • Confidential computing depends on remote attestation: the chip signs a measurement of the code it is running, and keys are released only to enclaves matching an approved build.
  • Hardware enclaves are not invulnerable: Intel SGX suffered side-channel attacks such as Foreshadow (2018), so designs add patching, key rotation and defence in depth.
  • Differential privacy is tuned by a privacy-loss budget called epsilon: smaller values add more noise and give stronger privacy, and every query spends part of the budget.
  • Apple's Private Cloud Compute publishes its server software images for researchers, and iPhones refuse to send requests to servers whose attested software is not in that public log.
  • Regulators now discuss PETs directly; the UK Information Commissioner's Office published PETs guidance in 2023, and advertising 'data clean rooms' use MPC or enclaves to match audiences.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling hashed or pseudonymised data 'anonymous'; hashed emails and phone numbers can be reversed by simply guessing and hashing candidates.
  • Assuming confidential computing removes all trust: you still trust the chip maker, its attestation service and the enclave code itself.
  • Reaching for fully homomorphic encryption when access control, MPC or an enclave would meet the need far more cheaply.
  • Treating differential privacy as a one-off setting; unmanaged repeated queries exhaust the privacy budget and can reveal individuals.

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example Homomorphic encryptionAcademic research; deployed by Apple, Microsoft, Google · Technique · Emerging Lets a server calculate on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer that only you can decrypt. Apple uses homomorphic encryption for Live Caller ID Lookup and Enhanced Visual Search, so its servers never see what is being looked up. Microsoft SEAL / OpenFHEMicrosoft / OpenFHE community (Duality and partners) · Library · Emerging Open-source libraries implementing homomorphic encryption schemes such as BFV and CKKS for developers. A research team uses OpenFHE to compute statistics on encrypted genomic data hosted by a cloud provider. Secure multi-party computation (MPC)Academic research; Google, Partisia and others · Technique · Emerging Several parties jointly compute a result, such as an average, while each keeps its own input secret. Boston-area employers measured their gender pay gap with MPC, without any company revealing individual salaries. Zero-knowledge proofsZcash, Ethereum zk-rollups (zkSync, Starknet), Google · Technique · Emerging Prove a statement is true, such as 'over 18' or 'valid transaction', without revealing the underlying data. Zcash hides transaction details; zk-rollups bundle thousands of Ethereum transactions into one proof; Google open-sourced ZK code for age assurance. Private set intersection (PSI)Google, Apple, Microsoft and others · Technique · Recommended Two parties learn which items they have in common without revealing the rest of their lists. Google Password Checkup and Apple's password monitoring compare your saved passwords with breach lists without revealing them. Privacy Pass / Private Access TokensIETF (RFC 9576-9578); Apple, Cloudflare · Protocol · Recommended Unlinkable tokens proving 'this is a genuine device or person' so sites can skip CAPTCHAs without tracking you. An iPhone user visiting a Cloudflare-protected site skips the CAPTCHA because Safari presents a Private Access Token. Oblivious HTTPIETF (RFC 9458) · Protocol · Recommended Routes a request through a relay that knows who you are but not what you ask, while the server sees the question but not you. Chrome sends some Safe Browsing checks through an OHTTP relay, so Google learns the query but not the user's IP address. Key transparencyWhatsApp, Apple (Contact Key Verification) · Technique · Recommended Public, auditable logs of users' encryption keys so apps can detect a server secretly swapping in a fake key. WhatsApp rolled out key transparency in 2023; Apple's iMessage Contact Key Verification alerts users if an unknown device appears. Confidential computingIntel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, AWS Nitro Enclaves, Arm CCA · Technique · Emerging Hardware keeps data encrypted even while being processed in memory, hidden from the cloud operator, with remote proof (attestation). A bank runs fraud scoring inside AWS Nitro Enclaves; Apple's Private Cloud Compute serves AI requests on attested servers. Differential privacyApple, Google, US Census Bureau · Technique (related, not encryption) · Recommended Adds carefully measured random noise so trends can be studied without revealing any individual. The 2020 US Census used differential privacy, and Apple learns which emoji are popular without knowing who typed them. Quantum key distribution (QKD)ID Quantique, Toshiba; China's Micius satellite · Technology · Emerging Uses single particles of light to share keys and reveal eavesdroppers; needs special hardware and has distance limits. China demonstrated satellite QKD in 2017, but NSA and the UK's NCSC recommend post-quantum algorithms instead for most uses.

docs.title: 9.15 Media Encryption & DRM Technology
docs.text:
Streaming services, film studios and pay-TV companies encrypt films, music and live sport so only paying customers' approved devices can play them. DRM (digital rights management) systems hand out the decryption keys only to devices that follow the rules, such as blocking screen recording.

How a protected video gets its key. The content key is unwrapped only inside the device's DRM module (CDM); the app and browser never see it in clear.

Think of it like…

It is like a cinema that lets you watch the film but never lets you take the reel home: the projector holds the key, not you.

Real-world example

The fictional streaming service FlickHarbor encrypts each new series once using Common Encryption, then serves it to Android phones with Widevine, iPhones with FairPlay and Windows PCs with PlayReady. Each device requests a licence, proving it is a genuine, secure player before receiving the key. The 4K version goes only to devices with hardware-protected playback, and HDCP encrypts the picture on the cable to the TV. When a leaked copy appears online, an invisible watermark points to the account that recorded it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The studio or streamer encrypts the video with AES content keys.
  2. A licence server releases keys only to devices that prove they are approved players.
  3. The device decrypts inside a protected area, ideally in secure hardware.
  4. HDCP encrypts the signal on its way to the screen.
  5. Watermarks help trace any leak back to its source.

Who uses it

Streaming platforms, film and music studios, pay-TV and sports broadcasters, e-book stores and device makers.

Key takeaway

DRM slows piracy rather than stopping it: combine hardware-backed playback for premium content with forensic watermarking and leak monitoring.

Going deeper

  • CENC's 'cbcs' scheme encrypts video with AES-CBC in a pattern (one block in ten) and is supported by Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady, so one CMAF file serves both HLS and DASH players.
  • Widevine L1 decrypts and decodes inside a trusted execution environment, while L3 is software-only; most streamers cap L3 devices at standard definition.
  • Streamers use separate keys per title and per quality tier (SD, HD, UHD), and rotate keys on live channels, so one compromised device class does not unlock everything.
  • Live sport adds session-based forensic watermarking, where each viewer receives a unique mix of A/B video segments, because a leaked stream loses value within minutes.
  • Multi-DRM services run licence servers for all three major DRMs behind one API, so most streamers never operate their own licence infrastructure.
  • HDCP 2.x authenticates the screen with RSA, encrypts the picture with AES-128 in counter mode and runs a round-trip 'locality check' so the signal cannot be relayed far away.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting DRM to end piracy; screen capture and camera recording still happen, so watermarking and fast takedowns are essential.
  • Over-strict DRM that blocks paying customers on older TVs or browsers, raising support costs and pushing people towards pirate copies.
  • Encrypting a whole catalogue with one content key, so a single leaked key unlocks everything.

docs.text: Name What it does Example Google WidevineGoogle · DRM system · Recommended The DRM in Chrome, Android, Android TV and many smart TVs; its hardware-backed 'L1' level is required for HD and 4K on most services. A phone with Widevine L1 streams a series in HD, while a rooted phone falling back to software-only L3 gets standard definition. Apple FairPlay StreamingApple · DRM system · Recommended Apple's DRM for streaming video in Safari and on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV. Video apps on Apple TV use FairPlay so a film's keys are released only to genuine Apple devices. A sports broadcaster protects its live football streams on smart TVs and Xbox consoles with PlayReady licences. A streamer stores each episode once, encrypted in 'cbcs' mode, and serves it to every device type, saving storage and encoding costs. Encrypted Media Extensions (EME)W3C · Standard · Recommended Browser interface that lets a web page hand encrypted video to the browser's built-in DRM module, without plug-ins. Netflix in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari plays through EME, which replaced the old Silverlight and Flash plug-ins. A pirate restreams a boxing match; the watermark identifies the subscriber account within minutes and the stream is cut off.

docs.title: 9.16 Crypto Libraries Developers Use
docs.text:
Developers almost never write encryption maths themselves; they call well-tested libraries of code. Choosing a maintained, widely reviewed library and keeping it updated is one of the most important security decisions a software team makes.

Where crypto libraries sit in an app. Application code should touch only the top layers; the lower layers are where validated, constant-time, hardware-accelerated code lives.

Think of it like…

It is like fitting certified, crash-tested brakes from a reputable maker instead of welding your own in the garage.

Real-world example

The fictional fintech LedgerLoop writes its backend in Go using the standard crypto packages, while its mobile apps use Apple CryptoKit on iPhone and Google Tink on Android. Its load balancers use AWS-LC, which holds the FIPS 140-3 validation its US government customers demand. When an OpenSSL security advisory lands, automated tooling opens update requests the same day.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a mature library that fits your programming language and platform.
  2. Prefer high-level, hard-to-misuse APIs (such as Tink or libsodium) over raw building blocks.
  3. Use FIPS-validated builds when customers or regulators require them.
  4. Watch security advisories and update quickly.
  5. Plan for post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA), which are now arriving in libraries.

Who uses it

Software developers, DevOps teams, device makers and security engineers.

Key takeaway

Never implement algorithms yourself: use a high-level API from a maintained library and keep it patched.

Going deeper

  • OpenSSL 3 replaced 'engines' with 'providers': the FIPS provider is a separately validated module loaded by configuration, and a 'legacy' provider holds old algorithms such as MD4, RC4 and DES.
  • OpenSSL long-term-support releases get five years of fixes: 3.0 until September 2026 and 3.5 until April 2030, so products on 3.0 need upgrade plans now.
  • FIPS 140-3 validation covers a specific module version and build; a library's 'FIPS mode' is compliant only when that exact validated version runs in its approved configuration.
  • Good libraries are constant-time: comparisons and key operations avoid secret-dependent branches and memory lookups, so attackers cannot learn keys by timing responses.
  • Misuse-resistant APIs such as libsodium's secretbox and Tink's AEAD choose the algorithm, generate nonces and bundle authentication, removing the decisions developers most often get wrong.
  • Formally verified code is now mainstream: BoringSSL uses Fiat-Crypto, Firefox and the Linux kernel use HACL* code, and AWS-LC proves key routines correct with automated reasoning.
  • Dependency tools (Dependabot, Renovate, OSV-Scanner) and SBOMs reveal which services embed a vulnerable library version as soon as an advisory lands.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Copying old Stack Overflow snippets that use ECB, static IVs or MD5; follow the library's current documentation and safe recipes.
  • Statically bundling an old OpenSSL into a product and never updating it; track embedded copies through SBOMs and rebuild on advisories.
  • Assuming any library labelled 'FIPS' makes the whole product validated; only the tested module in its approved mode counts.
  • Mixing several crypto libraries with different defaults in one product, making algorithm choices inconsistent and upgrades hard.

docs.title: 9.17 Cryptographic Hardware
docs.text:
Keys stored as ordinary files can be copied by malware. Special security chips keep keys locked inside, do the cryptography themselves and never let the secret out; that is how Face ID, bank cards and laptop encryption stay safe.

Three kinds of key-protecting hardware

TPM Phone secure chip HSM Lives in PC motherboard or CPU firmware Phone or Mac system chip Data-centre appliance or cloud Typical keys Disk encryption, device identity Biometrics, passkeys, payments CA roots, payment, code signing Speed Slow: a few operations/second Moderate, per user Thousands of operations/second Physical protection Tamper-resistant chip Isolated processor, encrypted memory Sensors wipe keys on intrusion Cost Built in Built in Appliance or hourly cloud fee

All three keep keys inside tamper-resistant hardware; they differ in where they live, how fast they are and what they guard.

Think of it like…

It is like a bank teller behind bulletproof glass: you pass requests through the slot and get answers back, but you can never reach the cash drawer.

Real-world example

When Leo unlocks his iPhone with Face ID, the Secure Enclave checks the match and releases keys only if it succeeds. His work laptop's TPM holds the BitLocker key and refuses to release it if someone tampers with the startup process. At the office he signs into the VPN with a YubiKey, and the company's payroll signing keys live in a cloud HSM.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Keys are generated inside the chip and marked non-exportable.
  2. Apps send data in and ask the chip to sign, decrypt or verify.
  3. The chip checks a PIN, fingerprint or system health before using a key.
  4. Tamper sensors wipe secrets if someone attacks the hardware physically.
  5. Certifications (FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria) prove the protection was tested.

Who uses it

Phone and PC makers, banks, cloud providers, certificate authorities, governments and any company guarding high-value keys.

Key takeaway

Put your most valuable keys (CA, payment, code-signing and admin logins) in hardware so they cannot simply be copied.

Going deeper

  • FIPS 140-3 has four levels: Level 1 covers software modules, Level 2 adds tamper evidence and role-based login, Level 3 adds tamper resistance and identity-based login, Level 4 resists environmental attacks.
  • Applications reach HSMs and tokens through PKCS #11, Microsoft CNG key storage providers, Java JCE providers or KMIP, and cloud HSMs expose the same interfaces so software ports easily.
  • Discrete TPMs talk to the CPU over an LPC or SPI bus that cheap probes can sniff for BitLocker keys on TPM-only setups; a pre-boot PIN or integrated TPMs such as Microsoft Pluton close the gap.
  • Key attestation lets TPMs, Android Keystore and FIDO keys prove a key was generated inside genuine hardware, so servers can enforce 'hardware-only' credentials.
  • Banks and certificate authorities activate HSMs with 'm of n' quorums of smart cards, so no single administrator can use or export a root key alone.
  • Hardware is not magic: timing and fault-injection attacks such as TPM-Fail (2019) have extracted keys from certified chips, so firmware updates and layered controls still matter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Generating a key in software and then importing it into hardware 'for safety'; it was already exposed in memory, so generate keys inside the device.
  • Relying on TPM-only BitLocker for high-risk laptops; add a pre-boot PIN against bus sniffing and similar physical attacks.
  • Buying a single HSM with no backup or cluster partner; a hardware failure can mean permanently lost keys.
  • Believing a hardware-held key cannot be misused; malware on the host can still ask the chip to sign or decrypt on its behalf.

Mia checks the destination address on her hardware wallet's screen before pressing the button, defeating malware that swaps addresses.

docs.title: 9.18 Standards, Certifications & Compliance
docs.text:
Standards tell everyone which algorithms and key sizes are trustworthy and how to use them properly; certifications prove a product was tested against them. Governments, banks and large customers often refuse to buy products without them.

Compliance milestones to track. Standards change on fixed dates; procurement and audits follow them, so put these dates in the roadmap.

Think of it like…

It is like the safety rating on a car or the approval mark on a plug: you don't test every product yourself, you trust the certified label.

Real-world example

The fictional cloud startup NimbusVault wants a US federal contract, so it must use FIPS 140-3 validated crypto modules, manage keys following NIST SP 800-57 and plan its post-quantum move on NSA's CNSA 2.0 timeline. To serve European banks it also maps its controls to PCI DSS and supports eIDAS 2.0 qualified signatures. Its sales team now answers security questionnaires by pointing to certificates instead of promises.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify which rules apply: government, payments, telecom or regional law.
  2. Choose algorithms and modules already approved by those standards.
  3. Get products tested by accredited labs (FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria).
  4. Document key management and keep a cryptographic inventory.
  5. Track transition deadlines, especially for post-quantum migration.

Who uses it

Compliance officers, product managers, auditors, government buyers and vendors selling to regulated industries.

Key takeaway

Check the certificate, not the marketing: look up a product's FIPS or Common Criteria listing yourself.

Going deeper

  • CMVP validation queues often exceed a year, so vendors appear first on the 'Modules in Process' list; buyers should check certificate status and dates on NIST's CMVP search.
  • NIST SP 800-131A revision 3 (draft) proposes retiring SHA-1 and 224-bit hash functions by the end of 2030 and disallowing ECB mode for encryption.
  • Common Criteria assurance runs from EAL1 to EAL7; smart-card chips are usually certified at EAL5+ or EAL6+, while network products use collaborative Protection Profiles.
  • The EU's EUCC scheme, applying since February 2025, replaces national SOG-IS certificates with EU-wide certificates based on Common Criteria.
  • Auditors increasingly ask for a cryptographic inventory; DORA requires documented key management for EU financial firms, and US memo M-23-02 requires annual inventories at federal agencies.
  • Standards reference each other: PCI DSS points to NIST strength guidance, eIDAS to ETSI signature formats, and CNSA 2.0 to FIPS 203 and 204, so one change ripples widely.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Claiming 'FIPS compliant' because a product uses AES; only a validated module running in its approved mode counts.
  • Treating a passed audit as proof of security: standards set a minimum floor, not a ceiling.
  • Relying on FIPS 140-2 certificates after September 2026, when they became historical and no longer support new federal purchases.
  • Assuming one region's rules apply everywhere; China, Russia and South Korea require national algorithms in some sectors.

A cloud vendor selling to federal agencies supplies a list of every algorithm and key size in its product to support the agency's annual inventory.

docs.title: 9.19 Deprecated & Broken — What to Remove
docs.text:
Cryptography ages: computers get faster and researchers find flaws, so yesterday's 'secure' becomes today's open door. Organisations must hunt down old algorithms hiding in forgotten systems and replace them before attackers take advantage.

Remove this, replace with that

Remove Replace with Block ciphers DES, 3DES, Blowfish AES-128/256-GCM Stream ciphers RC4 ChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM Hashes in signatures MD5, SHA-1 SHA-256, SHA-384 Public keys RSA/DH-1024, export grade RSA-3072, P-256, X25519, then ML-KEM/ML-DSA TLS SSL, TLS 1.0/1.1, static RSA, CBC TLS 1.3, or TLS 1.2 ECDHE + AEAD Remote access Telnet, FTP, PPTP, ssh-rsa SSH with Ed25519, SFTP, WireGuard or IKEv2 Wi-Fi WEP, WPA-TKIP WPA3, or WPA2 with AES File encryption ZipCrypto, 40-bit Office/PDF AES-256 archives and documents

Most replacements already exist in every modern library, so the hard part is finding the old uses, not choosing the new ones.

Think of it like…

It is like replacing old locks that a locksmith has publicly shown can be opened with a paperclip: they still look like locks, but they no longer protect anything.

Real-world example

The fictional insurer HarborMutual scans its estate and finds TLS 1.0 on a forgotten partner portal, 3DES in a mainframe file transfer and MD5 'protecting' passwords in an old HR app. It fixes internet-facing systems first, moving the portal to TLS 1.3, file transfers to AES-256-GCM and HR passwords to Argon2id with forced resets. A quarterly scan makes sure the old algorithms never creep back.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inventory where cryptography is used: certificates, protocols, code and devices.
  2. Flag anything on the deprecated or broken list.
  3. Prioritise by exposure: internet-facing and sensitive-data systems first.
  4. Replace with modern equivalents and test compatibility with partners.
  5. Block the old algorithms in configuration so they cannot return.

Who uses it

Security architects, compliance teams, auditors and IT operations in every organisation.

Key takeaway

Build a cryptographic inventory: you cannot remove weak crypto you don't know about, and you will need it for post-quantum migration too.

Going deeper

  • Discovery comes first: test your own endpoints with SSL Labs or testssl.sh, inventory certificates from Certificate Transparency logs, and use code scanners such as Semgrep or CodeQL to find weak algorithm calls.
  • System-wide crypto policies block weak algorithms everywhere at once: Red Hat's update-crypto-policies (DEFAULT, FUTURE, FIPS) and Windows Group Policy cipher-suite ordering are common examples.
  • Prioritise by exposure: internet-facing protocols and signatures first, then stored data needing long confidentiality, then isolated internal systems protected by compensating controls.
  • Old protocol versions are covered in their own sections: SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1 under web transport, PPTP under VPNs, and WEP and WPA-TKIP under wireless networks.
  • ECB mode and unauthenticated CBC belong on removal lists even when the cipher is AES, because the mode, not the cipher, leaks patterns or allows padding-oracle attacks.
  • Legacy partners such as mainframes, medical devices and older banks may need years; isolate them, re-encrypt through gateways and set contractual deadlines.
  • Quantum computing will add RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography to this list around 2030-2035, so the inventory you build now serves both clean-ups.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Switching off an old algorithm without checking who still uses it; review logs of negotiated versions first, then disable in stages.
  • Assuming 'we use AES' means safe; AES in ECB mode, with reused nonces or with keys stored beside the data still fails.
  • Fixing configurations once and forgetting them; restores, vendor updates and new appliances can quietly re-enable weak options.
  • Keeping weak algorithms enabled 'for compatibility' with a client nobody can actually name.

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example DES, 3DES & other 64-bit-block ciphersIBM / NBS (DES, 1977); Blowfish and IDEA (1990s) · Block ciphers · Broken DES keys are brute-forced in hours; 64-bit blocks (3DES, Blowfish) leak data through Sweet32 on long sessions. NIST disallowed 3DES encryption after 2023. Look in payment key stores, mainframe file transfers, old VPN profiles and SNMPv3 settings. Use instead: AES-256-GCM, and AES key blocks in payment systems. RC4 leftovers (Kerberos, TLS, Wi-Fi, old files)Ron Rivest (1987) · Stream cipher · Broken Biased stream cipher still lurking in Kerberos RC4-HMAC tickets, old TLS settings, WPA-TKIP Wi-Fi and 40-bit Office and PDF protection. Microsoft turned RC4 off by default for Kerberos in 2026; audit accounts still requesting RC4 tickets first. Use instead: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. MD5 & SHA-1 in signatures and certificatesRon Rivest (MD5); NSA / NIST (SHA-1) · Hash functions · Broken Collision attacks let forgers make two documents share one signature; both still hide in internal CAs, code signatures, RADIUS and old password stores. Re-issue internal certificates and code signatures with SHA-256, and move MD5 password hashes to Argon2id at next login. Use instead: SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-3. RSA & Diffie-Hellman keys of 1024 bits or lessNIST SP 800-131A · Key sizes · Broken Only about 80-bit strength; the 2015 Logjam research suggested well-funded attackers could break widely shared 1024-bit Diffie-Hellman groups. Replace 1024-bit keys in old appliances, DKIM records and SSH host keys. Use instead: RSA-3072, ECDSA P-256 or X25519, then post-quantum hybrids. Export-grade ciphers1990s US export rules · Cipher suites · Broken Deliberately weakened 40-bit and 512-bit crypto; the FREAK and Logjam attacks (2015) forced servers back onto them. Remove all EXPORT and DHE-512 suites from server configs. Use instead: TLS 1.3 or TLS 1.2 ECDHE suites. Static RSA key exchange (TLS_RSA suites)TLS 1.2 and earlier · Cipher suites · Legacy The session secret is encrypted to the server's RSA key, so one stolen key decrypts all recorded traffic; also exposed to ROBOT-style padding attacks. TLS 1.3 removed it entirely; disable TLS_RSA_* suites on TLS 1.2 servers. Use instead: ECDHE key exchange, which gives forward secrecy. CBC-mode TLS cipher suitesTLS 1.2 and earlier · Cipher suites · Legacy Older MAC-then-encrypt CBC suites enabled BEAST, Lucky Thirteen and padding-oracle attacks; AEAD suites avoid this whole class of bugs. Mozilla's intermediate TLS profile already excludes CBC suites; keep them only for named legacy clients. Use instead: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 suites. Legacy SSH algorithmsOpenSSH and other SSH implementations · Protocol settings · Legacy SHA-1 'ssh-rsa' signatures, DSA keys, CBC ciphers and diffie-hellman-group1 key exchange; OpenSSH disabled ssh-rsa in 2021 and removed DSA in 2025. An audit flags network switches that only accept ssh-rsa; firmware updates enable rsa-sha2-256. Use instead: Ed25519 keys and hybrid post-quantum key exchange. Plain-text protocols (Telnet, FTP, HTTP, SNMPv1/v2c)1970s-1990s internet standards · Protocols · Broken Send passwords and data readable to anyone on the network path; still common on printers, switches, cameras and industrial equipment. Replace Telnet with SSH, FTP with SFTP, HTTP admin pages with HTTPS, and SNMPv1/v2c with SNMPv3 using authentication and AES privacy. ZipCrypto (legacy ZIP encryption)PKWARE (1989 ZIP format) · Stream cipher · Broken Original ZIP password protection; a known-plaintext attack recovers the keys when an attacker can guess a few bytes of any file inside. Some archive tools still default to ZipCrypto for compatibility; switch the setting. Use instead: AES-256 in 7-Zip or WinZip, with a long passphrase.

docs.title: 9.20 Common Crypto Mistakes Companies Make
docs.text:
Most real-world crypto failures aren't caused by broken maths; they come from using good algorithms badly: keys left in code, certificates nobody renews, passwords stored carelessly. These mistakes are common, cheap to prevent and very expensive when ignored.

Where real-world crypto fails. Almost every major incident traces back to one of these everyday mistakes rather than to a broken algorithm.

Think of it like…

It is like buying the world's best lock and then leaving the key under the doormat.

Real-world example

The fictional delivery app QuickCrate pushes code to a public GitHub repository with its payment API key inside, and within hours automated bots find it and run up fraudulent charges. The investigation also uncovers an expired certificate that took the app offline last spring and passwords hashed with plain SHA-1. QuickCrate adds secret scanning, a secrets vault, automated certificate renewal and Argon2id password hashing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Scan code and repositories for secrets before every commit.
  2. Store keys in a vault, KMS or HSM, never next to the data they protect.
  3. Use high-level libraries that handle nonces, randomness and modes for you.
  4. Automate and monitor certificate renewal.
  5. Have cryptographic designs reviewed by specialists before launch.

Who uses it

Developers, DevOps engineers, architects, security reviewers and technology leaders.

Key takeaway

Assume someone will eventually read your code, logs and backups: keys and secrets must never live there.

Going deeper

  • GitHub secret scanning with push protection blocks commits containing known token formats, and AWS automatically quarantines access keys it finds exposed in public repositories.
  • AES-GCM fails badly on nonce reuse: two messages under the same key and nonce leak their XOR and let attackers forge tags; with random 96-bit nonces, NIST limits one key to about 2^32 messages.
  • OWASP's password-storage advice: Argon2id with at least 19 MiB of memory and 2 iterations, bcrypt with cost 10 or more, or PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations where FIPS is required.
  • Root expiry causes outages too: when Let's Encrypt's old DST Root CA X3 expired in September 2021, older devices lacking the newer ISRG root suddenly failed to connect.
  • Logs and crash dumps are frequent leak points: mask tokens, avoid logging authorization headers and treat memory dumps from crypto services as secret material.
  • Test implementations against known-answer and edge-case vectors such as Project Wycheproof, which has caught subtle bugs in many widely used crypto libraries.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Deleting a leaked secret in a new commit and calling it fixed; it stays in history and forks, so revoke and rotate it immediately.
  • Using a password directly as an encryption key; derive keys with a proper KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt or PBKDF2.
  • Leaving 'temporary' test shortcuts like disabled certificate checks untracked; add lint rules or tests that fail if they reach production.
  • Assuming encryption hides message length and timing; sizes and traffic patterns can still reveal what was sent.

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example Hard-coded keys and secretsCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Passwords, API keys or encryption keys written directly into source code, config files or mobile apps. A cloud key pushed to a public repository is abused for crypto-mining within hours. Fix: secret scanning, a vault, and immediate key rotation. Nonce / IV reuseCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Reusing a 'number used once' with the same key, which can reveal plaintext or even the secret key. Sony's PS3 reused an ECDSA nonce, letting hackers compute its signing key (2010). Fix: libraries that manage nonces, or misuse-resistant AES-GCM-SIV. Rolling your own cryptoCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Inventing home-made algorithms or protocols instead of using vetted standards and libraries. A startup's homemade 'XOR encryption' of customer files is reversed in an afternoon. Fix: standard TLS plus libraries such as libsodium or Tink. Encoding mistaken for encryptionCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Treating Base64, hex or simple obfuscation as protection; anyone can reverse encoding instantly because it uses no key. A mobile app 'hides' its API secret in Base64; a curious user decodes it in seconds. Fix: keep secrets server-side and use real encryption. Unsalted or fast password hashesCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Storing passwords with plain MD5 or SHA-1 and no unique salt, so leaked hashes crack quickly. LinkedIn's 2012 breach exposed unsalted SHA-1 hashes, most later cracked. Fix: Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt with unique salts. Ignoring certificate validationCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Apps that accept any certificate, often a testing shortcut left in production, making TLS useless. A shopping app trusting any certificate lets a fake café hotspot read customers' logins. Fix: never disable verification; test TLS handling before release. Expired certificates causing outagesCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Certificates tracked manually in spreadsheets, forgotten until they expire and break services. An expired certificate took Microsoft Teams offline in February 2020. Fix: automate renewal with ACME and alert well before expiry. Weak random numbersCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Generating keys or tokens from predictable sources like time, simple counters or non-cryptographic random functions. A 2008 Debian OpenSSL bug left only 32,768 possible keys, forcing mass replacement. Fix: use the operating system's secure random generator. Storing keys next to the dataCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Keeping the encryption key in the same server, database or backup as the encrypted data. Thieves copy a database backup with its key in the same folder, so encryption achieves nothing. Fix: keys in a KMS or HSM with separate access. Encryption without integrityCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Using modes like AES-CBC without a message authentication code, so attackers can alter or probe ciphertext. Padding-oracle attacks have decrypted web cookies protected only by unauthenticated CBC. Fix: authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Timing leaks in secret comparisonsCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Checking tokens, MACs or passwords with ordinary string equality, which stops at the first wrong character and leaks timing clues. An API compares webhook signatures with '=='; switching to a constant-time compare (hmac.compare_digest or crypto/subtle) closes the leak. No crypto inventory or agilityCommon anti-pattern · Mistake · Broken Not knowing where algorithms, keys and certificates are used, making any change slow and risky. When a CA is distrusted, a firm spends months finding affected systems. Fix: keep a cryptographic bill of materials and design for swappable algorithms.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Cryptography — The Building Blocks
docs.text: Cryptography is the toolkit of locks, keys, seals and fingerprints that keeps digital life private and trustworthy. Meet Alice and Bob, who want to talk secretly, and Eve, who is listening: every algorithm here helps them hide messages, prove who they are, spot tampering or look after their keys. Each entry is labelled Recommended, Acceptable, Legacy, Broken, Regional or Emerging so you know what is safe to choose.

docs.title: 8.1 Symmetric Block Ciphers
docs.text:
A block cipher scrambles data in fixed-size chunks ("blocks", usually 16 bytes) using a secret key. It is called symmetric because the same key locks and unlocks the data, so both sides must already share it.

Inside one AES encryption. AES-128 repeats the round 10 times, AES-192 12 and AES-256 14; the final round skips MixColumns.

Think of it like…

Think of a lockbox where Alice and Bob each hold an identical copy of the same key: whatever Alice locks, only someone with that key can open.

Real-world example

Northwind Clinic stores patient records on a laptop. The laptop's disk encryption uses AES-256 with a key protected by the device's security chip. When the laptop is stolen from a car, the thief sees only scrambled bytes. The clinic reports a lost device, but no patient data is exposed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Alice and Bob agree on a secret key (often delivered using public-key cryptography).
  2. The message is cut into equal-sized blocks.
  3. Each block goes through many rounds of mixing and substitution driven by the key.
  4. A 'mode of operation' (see later section) chains the blocks together safely.
  5. Bob runs the same steps in reverse with the same key to get the original back.

Who uses it

Every operating system, browser, VPN, bank, cloud provider and phone uses block ciphers, AES above all, to protect stored and transmitted data.

Key takeaway

Use AES (128 or 256-bit key) in an authenticated mode such as GCM; avoid DES, 3DES and other 64-bit-block ciphers.

Going deeper

  • Block size matters as much as key size: 64-bit-block ciphers such as DES, 3DES, Blowfish and IDEA start repeating blocks after roughly 32 GB under one key, the weakness behind the 2016 Sweet32 attack.
  • AES-128 offers 128-bit security, far beyond brute force; Grover's quantum algorithm roughly halves effective key strength, which is why NSA's CNSA 2.0 requires AES-256 for national-security systems.
  • AES-NI instructions (Intel and AMD since about 2010) and ARMv8 crypto extensions run AES at several gigabytes per second per core and avoid the cache-timing leaks of table-based software.
  • AES is a substitution-permutation network; DES, Blowfish, Camellia and SM4 use Feistel-style structures that split the block and swap halves each round, so the same circuit can decrypt.
  • AES is specified in FIPS 197 (2001, editorially updated 2023) and ISO/IEC 18033-3; FIPS 140-3 modules must use implementations tested by NIST's Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program.
  • A block cipher alone encrypts just one block; real-world security comes from pairing it with a sound mode such as GCM plus careful key and nonce handling (see the next sections).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing AES-128 is weak; it is unbroken in practice, and AES-256 is chosen mainly for long-term or quantum-cautious requirements.
  • Encrypting without authentication, so ciphertext can be silently altered; use an AEAD mode or add a MAC.
  • Using a password directly as the key; generate random keys or derive them with a password-based KDF such as Argon2id or PBKDF2.

docs.title: Try it: Encrypt and decrypt a local test file with AES-256 (password-based key via PBKDF2)
docs.text:
echo "hello Bob" > secret.txt
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -salt -in secret.txt -out secret.enc
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in secret.enc

Messages encrypted with PGP 2.x in the 1990s used IDEA; modern OpenPGP software uses AES.

docs.title: 8.2 Stream Ciphers
docs.text:
A stream cipher turns a secret key into an endless stream of random-looking bytes (a "keystream") and mixes it with the message one byte at a time. It is fast and handles data of any length, but the same key and starting value must never be reused.

How ChaCha20 encrypts. Reuse the same key and nonce and the two keystreams cancel under XOR, exposing both messages.

Think of it like…

It is like a pair of identical 'magic pads' of random numbers: Alice adds the pad to her message, Bob subtracts the same pad, and anyone without the pad sees noise.

Real-world example

Bob's phone at a café connects to his company VPN, Kestrel Tech, using WireGuard. WireGuard always encrypts with the ChaCha20 stream cipher, which runs fast in plain software and is kind to the battery. A snooper on the café Wi-Fi captures only scrambled packets.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Both sides share a secret key plus a unique 'nonce' (a number used once) for each message.
  2. The cipher expands key + nonce into a long keystream.
  3. Each byte of the message is combined (XOR) with the next keystream byte.
  4. The receiver generates the identical keystream and reverses the combination.
  5. A separate authenticator (MAC) should be added so tampering is detected.

Who uses it

Mobile networks, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chips, VPNs, messaging apps and TLS on phones rely on stream ciphers.

Key takeaway

Never reuse a key+nonce pair, and always pair a stream cipher with authentication (for example ChaCha20-Poly1305).

Going deeper

  • Ciphertext equals plaintext XOR keystream, so two messages encrypted with the same keystream let an eavesdropper XOR the ciphertexts and obtain the XOR of both plaintexts, the classic 'two-time pad' failure.
  • ChaCha20 uses only 32-bit additions, rotations and XORs (an 'ARX' design) over 20 rounds, which makes fast, constant-time software easy on chips without AES hardware.
  • Nonce sizes: ChaCha20 in RFC 8439 uses a 96-bit nonce, safe with a counter; XChaCha20's 192-bit nonce is safe to pick at random; AES-GCM with random 96-bit nonces is limited to about 2^32 messages per key.
  • Any block cipher in counter (CTR) mode behaves like a stream cipher, which is exactly how AES-GCM encrypts; see the Modes of Operation section.
  • 4G and 5G radio encryption uses three algorithm families: SNOW 3G (EEA1/EIA1), AES (EEA2/EIA2) and ZUC (EEA3/EIA3); 3GPP has also studied 256-bit successors for future networks.
  • Europe's eSTREAM project (2004-2008) picked software-oriented ciphers (HC-128, Rabbit, Salsa20/12, SOSEMANUK) and hardware-oriented ones (Grain, MICKEY, Trivium).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reusing a nonce 'because the messages are short'; a single repeat under the same key can reveal both plaintexts.
  • Believing encryption stops tampering; flipping a ciphertext bit flips the same plaintext bit, so always add a MAC or use an AEAD.
  • Building a home-made keystream from a hash or random() function; use a vetted cipher from a standard library.

docs.title: Try it: Encrypt and decrypt a local test file with the ChaCha20 stream cipher
docs.text:
echo "meet at noon" > notes.txt
openssl enc -chacha20 -pbkdf2 -salt -in notes.txt -out notes.enc
openssl enc -d -chacha20 -pbkdf2 -in notes.enc

The NaCl and libsodium 'secretbox' function uses XSalsa20 to encrypt small messages between apps. Chinese mobile operators encrypt LTE and 5G radio traffic with ZUC-based 128-EEA3. WEP Wi-Fi keys protected by RC4 could be cracked in minutes with free tools. Researchers showed intercepted 2G calls could be decrypted using precomputed A5/1 tables on ordinary hardware. docs.title: 8.3 Modes of Operation & Authenticated Encryption
docs.text:
A block cipher only scrambles one 16-byte block; a "mode" is the recipe for safely encrypting long messages with it, and the best modes ("authenticated encryption", AEAD) both hide the message and detect any tampering. The famous 'ECB penguin' shows why the recipe matters: encrypt a picture of Tux, the Linux penguin, block-by-block with the naive ECB mode and the penguin's outline is still clearly visible. That happens because identical patches of colour turn into identical scrambled patches, so the patterns leak.

Three modes compared

ECB CBC GCM (AEAD) Hides patterns No (ECB penguin) Yes Yes Detects tampering No No, needs a MAC Yes, 128-bit tag IV / nonce None Random, unpredictable IV Unique 96-bit nonce Parallel encryption Yes No Yes Padding needed Yes Yes No Verdict Broken Acceptable with MAC Recommended

Only an AEAD mode such as GCM both hides patterns and detects tampering.

Think of it like…

Encryption is an opaque envelope; authentication is the wax seal on it. AEAD gives you both, so Bob knows nobody read or swapped the letter.

Real-world example

Harbor Bank's mobile app sends payment instructions using TLS 1.3 with AES-GCM. Mallory, on the same network, flips a few bits trying to change the amount. The GCM authentication tag no longer matches, so the bank's server rejects the message instead of processing a fake payment.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick an AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for most uses).
  2. Generate a fresh, unique nonce/IV for every message.
  3. Encrypt the data and compute an authentication tag over it (plus any unencrypted headers).
  4. Send ciphertext, nonce and tag together.
  5. The receiver checks the tag first and refuses to decrypt anything that fails.

Who uses it

Protocol designers, developers, storage and disk-encryption vendors, payment processors and anyone choosing a cipher setting.

Key takeaway

Default to AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 with unique nonces; never use ECB, and never ship encryption without integrity checks.

Going deeper

  • AEAD means Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data: headers such as packet numbers can be authenticated without being encrypted, and the receiver verifies the tag before releasing any plaintext.
  • GCM limits: with random 96-bit nonces NIST advises at most 2^32 messages per key, and a single nonce repeat can expose the authentication key, letting attackers forge messages.
  • Encrypt-then-MAC is the safe way to combine a non-AEAD mode with a MAC; the MAC-then-encrypt order in old TLS CBC suites enabled padding-oracle attacks such as Lucky Thirteen.
  • XTS protects disks without authentication because sectors have no spare room for tags; tampering produces random garbage rather than a clear error.
  • Nonce-misuse-resistant modes (AES-GCM-SIV) and 'key-committing' AEAD designs are growing because ordinary AEAD ciphertext can sometimes decrypt validly under two different keys.
  • Format-preserving encryption (FF1) keeps data shape, such as 16 digits, so legacy systems work; small input domains weaken it, so NIST sets minimum domain sizes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reusing a GCM nonce after a reboot or counter reset; nonces must never repeat under the same key.
  • Acting on decrypted data before checking the tag; streaming code must verify authenticity before releasing plaintext.
  • Accepting a library default mode; Java's Cipher.getInstance("AES") means AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding, so always specify the mode explicitly.

docs.title: Try it: Compare encrypting the same file in CBC and CTR modes (openssl enc does not support GCM)
docs.text:
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in report.txt -out report.cbc
openssl enc -aes-256-ctr -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in report.txt -out report.ctr

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)NIST SP 800-38D · AEAD mode · Recommended AES in counter mode plus a fast authenticator; the most widely used authenticated encryption on the internet. Most HTTPS connections, IPsec VPNs and cloud storage services encrypt with AES-128-GCM or AES-256-GCM. ChaCha20-Poly1305IETF RFC 8439 · AEAD construction · Recommended ChaCha20 encryption sealed with a Poly1305 tag; fast in software and safe on devices without AES hardware. Google Chrome on Android, WireGuard and TLS 1.3 offer ChaCha20-Poly1305 for mobile traffic. AES-CCMNIST SP 800-38C; RFC 3610 · AEAD mode · Recommended Counter mode plus CBC-MAC; compact to implement, popular in wireless and low-power standards. WPA2's CCMP Wi-Fi encryption and TLS AES-CCM cipher suites protect each packet with AES-CCM. BitLocker on Windows, Apple FileVault and Linux LUKS encrypt whole drives with XTS-AES. AES-GCM-SIVIETF RFC 8452 · AEAD mode (nonce-misuse resistant) · Recommended A GCM variant that stays safe even if a nonce is accidentally repeated, leaking only whether identical messages repeated. Libraries such as Google Tink offer AES-GCM-SIV for systems where many servers encrypt independently and accidental nonce repeats are hard to rule out. CBC (Cipher Block Chaining)NIST SP 800-38A · Mode · Acceptable Each block is mixed with the previous one; widely used for decades but vulnerable to 'padding oracle' attacks without a MAC. Legacy TLS 1.0-1.2 suites and many file formats use AES-CBC; TLS 1.3 removed CBC entirely. CTR (Counter Mode)NIST SP 800-38A · Mode · Acceptable Encrypts a counter to make a keystream; fast and parallel but gives no tamper protection on its own. SRTP voice calls use AES in counter mode together with a separate HMAC authentication tag. Some VPN and storage tools offer AES-OCB, and OpenPGP's latest specification (RFC 9580) includes it. ECB (Electronic Codebook)NIST SP 800-38A · Mode · Broken Encrypts every block separately, so identical input blocks give identical output; patterns leak, as the 'ECB penguin' picture shows. The 2013 Adobe breach exposed passwords encrypted with 3DES-ECB; identical passwords produced identical ciphertext, so millions were guessed. Cloud KMS and HSMs export a data key 'wrapped' under a master key using AES-KW. A retailer tokenises card numbers with FF1 so legacy databases expecting 16 digits keep working. Teams using FF3-1 for masking test data are being advised to migrate to FF1.

docs.title: 8.4 Public-Key Encryption & Key Exchange
docs.text:
Public-key cryptography uses a pair of keys: a public key you can share with the world and a private key you keep secret. It lets two strangers agree on a shared secret, or send each other sealed messages, without ever meeting to swap a key first.

X25519 key agreement. Eve sees both public keys but cannot compute the shared secret without one of the private keys.

Think of it like…

Your public key is an open padlock you hand out freely; anyone can snap it shut on a box, but only your private key opens it. Key exchange is like Alice and Bob each mixing a secret paint colour into a shared public colour, swapping the mixtures, and both ending up with the same final colour that an eavesdropper cannot reproduce.

Real-world example

When Alice opens her bank's website, her browser and the bank's server run an X25519 key exchange inside TLS. Within milliseconds they agree on a fresh secret AES key without sending it over the network. Eve, watching the Wi-Fi, sees both public halves but cannot compute the secret.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each party generates a key pair and publishes the public half.
  2. For key exchange, each side combines its private key with the other's public key.
  3. Both arrive at the same shared secret, which is fed into a key-derivation function.
  4. The derived key then encrypts the actual data with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES.
  5. For encryption schemes (RSA, ECIES, HPKE), the sender uses the recipient's public key directly.

Who uses it

Web browsers, messaging apps, VPNs, email encryption, SSH, payment systems and mobile networks.

Key takeaway

Prefer elliptic-curve key exchange (X25519 or P-256), combined with ML-KEM for quantum safety; RSA should be at least 2048 (preferably 3072) bits.

Going deeper

  • Equal strength needs very different sizes: about 128-bit security takes 3072-bit RSA or DH but only a 256-bit elliptic-curve key; RSA-2048 gives about 112 bits, NIST's current minimum.
  • Forward secrecy: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key transport, so every session uses fresh ephemeral (EC)DHE keys and stealing the server's long-term key later cannot decrypt recorded traffic.
  • RSA encryption must use OAEP padding; the older PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding enables Bleichenbacher padding-oracle attacks, which resurfaced in 2017 as ROBOT against TLS servers.
  • A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) generates a random secret and 'encapsulates' it to the recipient's public key; ML-KEM and HPKE both follow this pattern.
  • Public-key maths is slow, so real systems are hybrid: public-key cryptography agrees on or wraps a symmetric key, and AES or ChaCha20 encrypts the actual data.
  • Key exchange alone does not prove identity; an unauthenticated exchange allows man-in-the-middle attacks, so TLS signs the handshake with the server's certificate key.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Encrypting large files directly with RSA; it can only handle a few hundred bytes, so use hybrid encryption.
  • Assuming a key exchange proves who is on the other end; without signatures or certificates, Eve can sit in the middle.
  • Keeping 1024-bit RSA or DH keys; they fall below current minimums and are considered within reach of well-funded attackers.

docs.title: Try it: Alice and Bob derive the same shared secret with X25519 (local files only; both lines print the same fingerprint)
docs.text:
openssl genpkey -algorithm X25519 -out alice.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm X25519 -out bob.key
openssl pkey -in alice.key -pubout -out alice.pub
openssl pkey -in bob.key -pubout -out bob.pub
openssl pkeyutl -derive -inkey alice.key -peerkey bob.pub | openssl dgst -sha256
openssl pkeyutl -derive -inkey bob.key -peerkey alice.pub | openssl dgst -sha256

Many HTTPS certificates still carry 2048-bit RSA keys; RSA-OAEP encrypts small secrets such as keys. A TLS 1.3 connection using curve P-256 performs ECDH so each session gets a fresh key. X25519Daniel J. Bernstein; RFC 7748 · Key exchange · Recommended ECDH on Curve25519, designed to be fast and hard to implement wrongly; the internet's most common key exchange. Signal, WhatsApp, WireGuard, SSH and most TLS 1.3 connections use X25519. Organisations wanting roughly 224-bit security can enable X448 in TLS 1.3 servers. docs.title: 8.5 Elliptic Curves in Use
docs.text:
Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) uses the mathematics of a special curved shape to make keys that are small but strong. A 256-bit curve key is about as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key. The "curve" is a fixed, published set of parameters that everyone agrees to use.

Key sizes for equal strength. Elliptic-curve keys grow gently as security rises, while RSA keys balloon (NIST SP 800-57).

Think of it like…

A curve is like a standard lock design: everybody uses the same blueprint, but each person's key cut is unique. Choosing a curve is choosing which trusted blueprint to build on.

Real-world example

Pinewood Software signs its Windows installer with a P-256 code-signing certificate, while its developers log in to servers with Ed25519 SSH keys built on Curve25519. Meanwhile the finance team's crypto wallet signs transactions on secp256k1. Three curves, each chosen for its own ecosystem.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A standards body publishes the curve's parameters.
  2. A private key is just a large random number.
  3. The public key is computed from it by 'multiplying' a standard point on the curve.
  4. Reversing that step (finding the private key from the public one) is infeasible.
  5. The keys are then used for key exchange (ECDH) or signatures (ECDSA, EdDSA).

Who uses it

TLS certificates, smart cards, passports, cryptocurrencies, SSH, phones and secure messaging.

Key takeaway

Use well-studied curves (P-256, P-384, Curve25519); all of them will eventually need post-quantum companions.

Going deeper

  • Curve shapes differ: NIST P-curves use short Weierstrass form, Curve25519 is a Montgomery curve suited to fast X25519, and its twisted-Edwards twin Edwards25519 powers Ed25519 signatures.
  • The NIST P-curves were generated from unexplained seed values, prompting 'nothing-up-my-sleeve' alternatives like Curve25519 and Brainpool, although no weakness in the P-curves has been found.
  • FIPS 186-5 and NIST SP 800-186 (2023) added Curve25519/Edwards25519 and Curve448 to the US-approved list alongside P-256, P-384 and P-521.
  • Invalid-curve and small-subgroup attacks hit software that fails to validate received points; X25519 was designed so any 32-byte input is safe to process.
  • Public keys are tiny: a compressed P-256 key is 33 bytes (65 uncompressed) and an X25519 key is 32 bytes, compared with 256 bytes for an RSA-2048 modulus.
  • Shor's algorithm on a large quantum computer would break every elliptic curve; estimates suggest 256-bit curves may need fewer qubits to break than RSA-2048.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking a 256-bit ECC key is weaker than 2048-bit RSA; it is stronger, roughly 128-bit versus 112-bit security.
  • Choosing secp256k1 or Brainpool where broad compatibility matters; most browsers only support P-256, P-384 and X25519 in TLS.
  • Confusing curves with algorithms: Curve25519 is the curve, X25519 does key exchange and Ed25519 signs, and their key formats differ.

docs.title: Try it: List the curves your OpenSSL knows and create a P-256 key
docs.text:
openssl ecparam -list_curves
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out p256.key
