docs.title: 8.6 Digital Signatures
docs.text:
A digital signature proves who created a piece of data and that it has not been changed since. The signer uses a private key; anyone can check the signature with the matching public key.

Sign once, verify anywhere. Anyone with the public key can verify, but only the private-key holder could have signed.

Think of it like…

It is a wax seal with a unique emblem: only the king owns the signet ring, but every citizen can recognise the seal and see if it was broken.

Real-world example

Riverbend Health pushes a software update to its medical tablets. The update is signed with the vendor's Ed25519 private key, and each tablet checks the signature before installing. When an attacker tries to slip in a modified update, the signature check fails and the tablet refuses it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The signer computes a hash (fingerprint) of the document.
  2. The hash is transformed with the signer's private key to create the signature.
  3. The document and signature are sent together.
  4. The verifier recomputes the hash and checks it against the signature using the public key.
  5. A certificate (from a trusted authority) links the public key to a real identity.

Who uses it

Certificate authorities, software vendors, banks, e-government, blockchain networks, email and document-signing services.

Key takeaway

Prefer Ed25519, ECDSA P-256 or RSA-PSS today, plan for ML-DSA, and never reuse random values (nonces) when signing.

Going deeper

  • Signatures provide integrity, authentication and non-repudiation; a MAC provides only the first two, because both parties share the key and either could have produced the tag.
  • Typical sizes: Ed25519 signatures are 64 bytes with 32-byte public keys; ECDSA P-256 about 64-72 bytes; RSA-2048 signatures 256 bytes; post-quantum ML-DSA-65 signatures 3,309 bytes.
  • ECDSA needs a fresh secret nonce for every signature; reuse or even slight bias leaks the private key, which is why deterministic nonces (RFC 6979) or EdDSA are preferred.
  • Legal e-signatures build on these schemes: EU eIDAS qualified electronic signatures and PDF PAdES or XML XAdES formats wrap RSA or ECDSA signatures with certificates and timestamps.
  • Trusted timestamps (RFC 3161) prove a signature existed before its certificate expired or was revoked, keeping signed contracts and code verifiable for many years.
  • Quantum-resistant signatures such as ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS/XMSS are covered in the Post-Quantum section; many systems will carry classic and post-quantum signatures side by side during migration.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using 'textbook' RSA or a home-made scheme; always use a vetted scheme such as RSA-PSS, ECDSA or Ed25519 from a library.
  • Checking that a signature is valid but not whose key made it; an attacker's correctly signed file is still malicious.
  • Assuming a signature hides the content; it proves origin and integrity, but the document stays readable unless also encrypted.

docs.title: Try it: Sign and verify a local file with Ed25519
docs.text:
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out signer.key
openssl pkey -in signer.key -pubout -out signer.pub
openssl pkeyutl -sign -rawin -inkey signer.key -in contract.txt -out contract.sig
openssl pkeyutl -verify -rawin -pubin -inkey signer.pub -in contract.txt -sigfile contract.sig

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example RSA-PSSRSA Labs; PKCS #1 v2.1 / RFC 8017 · Signature scheme · Recommended The modern, provably safer padding method for RSA signatures; required for RSA in TLS 1.3 handshakes. A TLS 1.3 server with an RSA certificate signs its handshake using RSA-PSS. RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signaturesRSA Labs; RFC 8017 · Signature scheme · Acceptable The classic RSA signature padding; no practical break when implemented correctly, and still used in most certificates. Most website certificates are signed by their authority with 'sha256WithRSAEncryption' (PKCS#1 v1.5). ECDSAANSI X9.62; NIST FIPS 186-5 · Signature scheme · Recommended Signatures on elliptic curves such as P-256; compact and fast, but a repeated random nonce leaks the private key. Sony's PlayStation 3 signing key leaked in 2010 because Sony reused the same ECDSA nonce. Ed25519Bernstein et al.; RFC 8032 · Signature scheme (EdDSA) · Recommended Fast, deterministic signatures on Curve25519 that avoid the nonce mistakes possible with ECDSA. OpenSSH creates Ed25519 keys by default; Git commit signing and Tor onion-service addresses also rely on Ed25519. Ed448RFC 8032 · Signature scheme (EdDSA) · Acceptable EdDSA on Curve448 for a higher security level; less widely supported than Ed25519. Some long-lived document-signing or PKI deployments choose Ed448 for its larger margin. Schnorr signatures (BIP-340)Claus Schnorr; Bitcoin BIP-340 · Signature scheme · Acceptable A simple, elegant signature scheme whose patent expired in 2008; supports combining several signers into one signature. Bitcoin's 2021 Taproot upgrade introduced BIP-340 Schnorr signatures for cheaper multi-party wallets. BLS signaturesBoneh, Lynn & Shacham · Signature scheme · Acceptable Short signatures that can be aggregated: thousands of signatures combine into one that verifies quickly. Ethereum's proof-of-stake consensus aggregates validator votes with BLS signatures on BLS12-381. DSANIST FIPS 186 (1991) · Signature scheme · Legacy The original US government signature standard; FIPS 186-5 (2023) no longer approves it for creating new signatures. OpenSSH disabled DSA (ssh-dss) keys by default in 2015 and removed DSA support entirely in OpenSSH 10.0 (2025). Deterministic ECDSA (RFC 6979)Thomas Pornin; IETF RFC 6979 (2013) · Technique · Recommended Derives each ECDSA nonce from the private key and message hash, so signing no longer depends on a good random generator. Hardware crypto wallets sign transactions with RFC 6979 nonces, so a weak random generator cannot leak the owner's key.

docs.title: 8.7 Post-Quantum Cryptography
docs.text:
A future large quantum computer could break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) uses different maths problems believed to resist both normal and quantum computers. The danger is "harvest now, decrypt later": a spy can record encrypted traffic today and simply wait until a quantum computer can open it.

The road to quantum-safe cryptography. Standards are done for key exchange and most signatures; the remaining deadlines are about migration.

Think of it like…

Imagine someone photocopying your locked diary today and storing it in a vault, betting that in ten years a master key will exist. PQC is changing the lock now, before that master key is built.

Real-world example

Atlas Insurance keeps customer medical claims secret for 30 years. Its security team learns that recorded traffic could be decrypted later, so it enables hybrid X25519MLKEM768 on its websites and VPNs. Browsers like Chrome and Firefox already support it, so most customers are protected without noticing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inventory where RSA and elliptic curves are used (TLS, VPN, SSH, code signing, PKI), ideally as a cryptographic bill of materials.
  2. Prioritise data that must stay secret for many years (harvest-now-decrypt-later risk).
  3. Turn on hybrid key exchange (classic + ML-KEM) in browsers, servers, SSH and VPNs.
  4. Plan to move signatures and certificates to ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or LMS/XMSS before regulators' deadlines (NIST's draft plan: RSA/ECC deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035).
  5. Build 'crypto agility' so algorithms can be swapped without rebuilding systems.

Who uses it

Governments, banks, telecoms, cloud and CDN providers, browser and OS vendors, and anyone protecting long-lived secrets.

Key takeaway

Enable hybrid ML-KEM key exchange now; signatures can follow, but key exchange is the urgent part because of harvest-now-decrypt-later.

Going deeper

  • Shor's algorithm efficiently factors numbers and solves discrete logarithms, breaking RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves; Grover's algorithm only halves symmetric strength, so AES-256 and SHA-384 remain safe.
  • ML-KEM comes in three sizes, 512, 768 and 1024; an ML-KEM-768 public key is 1,184 bytes and its ciphertext 1,088 bytes, versus 32 bytes for an X25519 public key.
  • Signature size drives migration pain: ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 signatures are 2,420, 3,309 and 4,627 bytes, and SLH-DSA signatures range from about 7.8 KB to 50 KB.
  • Hybrids combine a classic and a post-quantum algorithm so security holds if either survives; Germany's BSI and France's ANSSI favour hybrids, while NSA's CNSA 2.0 accepts ML-KEM-1024 alone.
  • Mosca's rule of thumb: if data must stay secret for X years and migration takes Y years, you are already late when X plus Y exceeds the years until a capable quantum computer.
  • Stateful hash-based signatures (LMS, XMSS) must never reuse a one-time key, so they suit firmware signing inside HSMs rather than general signing spread across many servers.
  • By 2026 hybrid ML-KEM key exchange is on by default in Chrome, Firefox, Apple platforms from iOS 26, Cloudflare and OpenSSH, and Signal and iMessage use post-quantum messaging protocols.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Waiting for a quantum computer to appear before acting; recorded traffic is already at risk and large migrations take many years.
  • Swapping algorithms without testing sizes; bigger keys and signatures can break packet limits, handshake buffers, smart cards and certificate size caps.
  • Assuming symmetric crypto must be replaced too; AES-256 and SHA-2/SHA-3 stay quantum-resistant, so focus on public-key algorithms.
  • Keeping early pre-standard Kyber versions; the final FIPS 203 ML-KEM is not wire-compatible, so upgrade to the standard version.

docs.title: Try it: Explore post-quantum algorithms (requires OpenSSL 3.5 or newer)
docs.text:
openssl list -kem-algorithms
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out pq-signer.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-KEM-768 -out pq-kem.key

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example ML-KEM (Kyber)NIST FIPS 203 (2024) · Post-quantum KEM · Recommended The main standard for quantum-resistant key agreement, based on lattice problems; fast with modest key sizes. Chrome, Firefox, Cloudflare, AWS and Apple iMessage (PQ3) use ML-KEM or Kyber to protect session keys. ML-DSA (Dilithium)NIST FIPS 204 (2024) · Post-quantum signature · Recommended The primary quantum-resistant signature standard, chosen for balanced speed and size; required by US CNSA 2.0. A device maker signs firmware with ML-DSA-87 to meet NSA CNSA 2.0 timelines. SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+)NIST FIPS 205 (2024) · Post-quantum signature · Recommended A hash-based signature relying only on hash-function security; very conservative but with large, slow signatures. A root certificate authority chooses SLH-DSA for keys that must stay trustworthy for decades. FN-DSA (Falcon)NIST draft FIPS 206 (final expected late 2026–2027) · Post-quantum signature · Emerging A lattice signature with much smaller signatures than ML-DSA, but tricky to implement safely; standard still being finalised. Designers of certificate chains and DNSSEC watch FN-DSA because small signatures save bandwidth. HQCNIST (selected March 2025; standard expected about 2027) · Post-quantum KEM · Emerging A code-based backup to ML-KEM, chosen so the world has an alternative built on different maths; its draft standard is still in progress. Standards teams plan HQC as a fallback in case lattice-based ML-KEM is ever weakened. Classic McElieceMcEliece (1978); ISO standardisation in progress · Post-quantum KEM · Emerging A 1978 code-based scheme that has never been broken, but has huge public keys of hundreds of kilobytes. Germany's BSI recommends Classic McEliece for long-term, high-security key exchange where large keys are acceptable. X25519MLKEM768 (hybrid TLS)IETF RFC 10024 (2026); deployed by Google, Mozilla, Apple, Cloudflare · Hybrid key exchange · Recommended Combines classic X25519 with ML-KEM-768 so the connection stays safe if either one holds. Chrome, Firefox and Apple devices (iOS 26 onwards) offer X25519MLKEM768 by default; Cloudflare reports a large share of its traffic is post-quantum protected. mlkem768x25519-sha256 (OpenSSH)OpenSSH project · Hybrid key exchange · Recommended OpenSSH's hybrid post-quantum key exchange, made the default in OpenSSH 10.0 (2025). An admin connecting from OpenSSH 10 to a modern server automatically gets post-quantum-protected SSH sessions. FrodoKEMMicrosoft Research & academic partners; ISO standardisation in progress · Post-quantum KEM · Emerging A conservative lattice KEM using simpler, less structured maths than ML-KEM; slower with bigger keys, but a cautious alternative. Germany's BSI and France's ANSSI list FrodoKEM as an option for organisations wanting an extra safety margin beyond ML-KEM. NIST IR 8547 transition timelineNIST (initial public draft, November 2024) · Migration guidance · Emerging Proposed US timeline: RSA and elliptic-curve algorithms at 112-bit strength deprecated after 2030, and all of them disallowed after 2035. Lakeside Credit Union schedules its VPN and certificate upgrades so nothing depends on RSA-2048 or P-256 alone by 2030. Cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM)OWASP CycloneDX 1.6 (2024) · Inventory technique · Recommended A machine-readable list of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols each application uses: the first step of quantum-safe migration. A scanner builds a CBOM for an insurer's apps, revealing 40 services still using RSA-1024 or SHA-1 that need upgrading.

docs.title: 8.8 Hash Functions
docs.text:
A hash function turns any amount of data into a short, fixed-size "fingerprint". Change a single comma and the fingerprint changes completely, and nobody can work backwards from the fingerprint to the data or find two inputs with the same fingerprint.

Why MD5 and SHA-1 were retired

MD5 SHA-1 SHA-256 Output size 128 bits 160 bits 256 bits First collision 2004 2017 (SHAttered) None known Chosen-prefix collision 2007 (used by Flame, 2012) 2020 ('Shambles') None known Safe for signatures No No Yes Still OK for Non-security checksums Legacy HMAC only Everything

Once attackers can craft two files with the same fingerprint, a hash is useless for signatures.

Think of it like…

It is a fingerprint for files: a tiny smudge identifies a whole person, and two different people should never share one.

Real-world example

Maya downloads a Linux installer from a mirror site. The official website publishes the file's SHA-256 fingerprint. Maya computes the fingerprint of her download, sees it matches exactly, and knows the file was not corrupted or swapped by an attacker on the mirror.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Feed any data (a file, password, message) into the hash function.
  2. It mixes the data through many rounds and outputs a fixed-size value, e.g. 256 bits.
  3. Publish or store that fingerprint.
  4. Later, recompute the hash and compare; any difference means the data changed.
  5. Hashes are building blocks for signatures, MACs, blockchains and password storage.

Who uses it

Software distributors, forensics teams, blockchain systems, version control (Git), certificate authorities and backup tools.

Key takeaway

Use SHA-256, SHA-384/512, SHA-3 or BLAKE2/3; never use MD5 or SHA-1 for security.

Going deeper

  • Three properties matter: preimage resistance (cannot reverse the hash), second-preimage resistance (cannot match a given input) and collision resistance (cannot find any two inputs with the same hash).
  • Birthday bound: an n-bit hash gives only about n/2 bits of collision resistance, so SHA-256 offers 128-bit collision security and SHA-1 at best 80 bits, even before its specific attacks.
  • SHA-2 is vulnerable to length extension: knowing H(secret‖message) lets an attacker compute the hash of a longer message; use HMAC, SHA-3 or SHA-512/256 rather than secret-prefix hashing.
  • SHA-3 uses a 'sponge' built on the 1600-bit Keccak-f permutation, a design entirely unlike SHA-2, so a breakthrough against one would not automatically hit the other.
  • Speed: SHA-256 has CPU instructions on modern Intel, AMD and ARM chips, while BLAKE3 uses SIMD and multiple cores to hash at several gigabytes per second.
  • Plain hashes are wrong for passwords (too fast) and for authentication (no key); use the password-hashing and MAC constructions in the following sections.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using MD5 'just for integrity' where an attacker can supply files; collisions let them swap content behind a matching fingerprint.
  • Hashing passwords with one round of SHA-256; GPUs test billions of guesses per second, so use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt.
  • Treating Keccak-256 and SHA3-256 as identical; their padding differs, so outputs never match and libraries must be chosen carefully.

docs.title: Try it: Fingerprint a local file with SHA-256 and SHA3-256
docs.text:
openssl dgst -sha256 report.pdf
openssl dgst -sha3-256 report.pdf

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example SHA-256NSA / NIST FIPS 180-4 · Hash function (SHA-2) · Recommended The workhorse 256-bit hash: used in certificates, signatures, software downloads and blockchains. Bitcoin mining, TLS certificates and Windows code signing all depend on SHA-256. SHA-384 / SHA-512NSA / NIST FIPS 180-4 · Hash function (SHA-2) · Recommended Longer SHA-2 variants with a bigger safety margin; SHA-512 is often faster on 64-bit CPUs. US CNSA suites require SHA-384; Linux password hashes ($6$) are built on SHA-512. SHA-3NIST FIPS 202 (based on Keccak) · Hash function · Recommended A completely different design from SHA-2, standardised in 2015 as a backup in case SHA-2 ever weakens. ML-KEM and ML-DSA use SHA-3 family functions internally; some HSMs offer SHA3-256 for signatures. SHAKE128 / SHAKE256NIST FIPS 202 · Extendable-output function (XOF) · Recommended SHA-3 relatives that can produce output of any length you ask for, useful for generating keys and masks. Post-quantum algorithms like ML-DSA and SLH-DSA use SHAKE to stretch seeds into large values. BLAKE2Aumasson, Neves, Wilcox-O'Hearn, Winnerlein; RFC 7693 · Hash function · Recommended Faster than MD5 yet secure; popular in modern software libraries. WireGuard, the Argon2 password hash and libsodium's generic hash function use BLAKE2. BLAKE3O'Connor, Aumasson, Neves, Wilcox-O'Hearn (2020) · Hash function · Acceptable An extremely fast, parallel hash built from BLAKE2 ideas; not a NIST or ISO standard. Backup and file-sync tools use BLAKE3 to fingerprint large files quickly across many CPU cores. Keccak-256Keccak team; Ethereum · Hash function · Acceptable The original Keccak before NIST's final SHA-3 padding tweak, so its output differs from SHA3-256. Ethereum derives account addresses and smart-contract function IDs with Keccak-256. RIPEMD-160Dobbertin, Bosselaers & Preneel (1996) · Hash function · Legacy An older 160-bit European hash; not broken, but its short output gives a smaller safety margin. Bitcoin addresses are made by hashing a public key with SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160. SM3Chinese State Cryptography Administration · Hash function · Regional China's national 256-bit hash, used with SM2 signatures; standardised in ISO/IEC 10118-3. Chinese digital certificates and e-government systems hash documents with SM3. StreebogRussian standard GOST R 34.11-2012 · Hash function · Regional Russia's national hash with 256 or 512-bit output, used with GOST digital signatures. Russian electronic tax filings and e-signatures use Streebog under national rules. SHA-1NSA / NIST (1995) · Hash function · Broken A 160-bit hash; in 2017 researchers made two different PDFs with the same SHA-1 ('SHAttered'). NIST retires it completely by end of 2030. Browsers stopped trusting SHA-1 certificates in 2017; Git is moving to SHA-256 repositories. MD5Ron Rivest (1992) · Hash function · Broken A fast 128-bit hash where collisions can be made in seconds; useless for security, fine only for non-security checksums. The Flame malware (2012) forged a Microsoft code-signing certificate using an MD5 collision.

docs.title: 8.9 Message Authentication Codes
docs.text:
A Message Authentication Code (MAC) is a short tag computed from a message and a shared secret key. If the message is changed, or the sender does not know the key, the tag will not match, so the receiver knows the message is genuine and untouched.

Verifying a signed webhook. The HMAC tag stops forgeries, and the signed timestamp stops replays of old genuine messages.

Think of it like…

It is like a secret handshake stamped on a parcel: only Alice and Bob know the handshake, so a parcel with the right stamp must have come from one of them and has not been repacked.

Real-world example

Copperleaf Payments sends webhook notifications to merchants' servers. Each notification carries an HMAC-SHA256 tag made with a secret shared with that merchant. When a fraudster sends a fake 'payment succeeded' message to a merchant's server, the tag does not verify and the order is not shipped.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Sender and receiver share a secret key.
  2. The sender computes a tag from the key and the message.
  3. Message and tag travel together.
  4. The receiver recomputes the tag with its copy of the key.
  5. If the tags match exactly (compared in constant time), the message is accepted.

Who uses it

API platforms, payment providers, cloud services, network protocols, token systems (JWT) and authenticator apps.

Key takeaway

Use HMAC-SHA256 or an AEAD mode, keep keys secret, and compare tags with a constant-time function.

Going deeper

  • HMAC computes H((K ⊕ opad) ‖ H((K ⊕ ipad) ‖ message)); the nested hashing defeats the length-extension attacks that break naive H(key ‖ message) designs.
  • HMAC-SHA256 tags are 32 bytes; truncating to 16 bytes (128 bits) is common and safe, while very short tags of 8 bytes or less need strict rate limits.
  • A MAC alone does not stop replays; include a timestamp, sequence number or nonce in the authenticated data and reject old or repeated values.
  • Compare tags with constant-time functions, such as Python's hmac.compare_digest or Node.js crypto.timingSafeEqual, because early-exit comparisons leak how many bytes matched.
  • Poly1305 and GMAC are fast universal-hash MACs that are only safe with a fresh key or unique nonce per message; a repeat can let attackers forge tags.
  • Anyone who can verify a MAC can also create one, so MACs suit two parties or a single system; signatures suit many independent verifiers.
  • Use HMAC keys at least as long as the security level you need, for example 32 random bytes for HMAC-SHA256, generated by a CSPRNG.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Building a MAC as SHA-256(secret + message); length extension makes it forgeable, so use HMAC or KMAC.
  • Comparing tags with ordinary string equality, which opens a timing side channel; use a constant-time comparison function.
  • Using the same key for encryption and authentication; derive separate keys with HKDF or simply use an AEAD mode.

docs.title: Try it: Compute an HMAC-SHA256 tag for a local file with a test key
docs.text: openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "test-only-secret" invoice.csv

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example HMAC-SHA256Bellare, Canetti & Krawczyk; RFC 2104 / FIPS 198-1 · MAC · Recommended Wraps SHA-256 with a secret key; the most widely used MAC on the internet. AWS request signing, Stripe webhooks and HS256 JSON Web Tokens use HMAC-SHA256. HMAC-SHA1RFC 2104 · MAC · Legacy HMAC with SHA-1; still not practically broken as a MAC, but being phased out with SHA-1. Many authenticator apps generate one-time codes (TOTP, RFC 6238) using HMAC-SHA1 by default. CMAC (AES-CMAC)NIST SP 800-38B; RFC 4493 · MAC · Recommended A MAC built from a block cipher like AES; handy where AES hardware exists but hashing is costly. Car networks (AUTOSAR SecOC) and Wi-Fi protected management frames (802.11w) authenticate messages with AES-CMAC. GMACNIST SP 800-38D · MAC · Acceptable The authentication-only part of AES-GCM, used when data must be verified but not hidden. Network switches using MACsec can run GMAC to authenticate Ethernet frames without encrypting them. Poly1305Daniel J. Bernstein; RFC 8439 · One-time MAC · Recommended A very fast authenticator that needs a fresh key for each message; usually paired with ChaCha20. In ChaCha20-Poly1305, every TLS or WireGuard packet gets its own Poly1305 tag. KMACNIST SP 800-185 · MAC · Recommended A MAC built on SHA-3 (Keccak), simpler than HMAC because SHA-3's design already resists length-extension tricks. SHA-3-based designs and HSMs use KMAC for authentication tags and for NIST SP 800-108 key derivation. SipHashAumasson & Bernstein (2012) · Short-input keyed hash · Recommended A fast keyed hash for short inputs, used to stop attackers flooding hash tables with colliding keys. Python, Rust and the Linux kernel use SipHash to defend hash tables against denial-of-service attacks. BLAKE2 / BLAKE3 keyed modeBLAKE2 and BLAKE3 teams; RFC 7693 · Keyed hash (MAC) · Recommended Both hashes accept a secret key directly, giving a fast, secure MAC without HMAC's two passes. WireGuard uses keyed BLAKE2s to compute the MAC fields on its handshake messages, cheaply rejecting forged packets.

docs.title: 8.10 Password Hashing & Key Derivation
docs.text:
Websites should store only a scrambled fingerprint of your password, never the password itself, and plain fast hashes (like SHA-256) are bad for this because attackers with stolen hashes can try billions of guesses per second. Password hashes are deliberately slow and memory-hungry, and each one is mixed with a random "salt" so identical passwords look different and pre-computed guess tables are useless. Key derivation functions (KDFs) turn a password or shared secret into proper encryption keys.

Storing a password with Argon2id. The stored string records the algorithm, costs and salt, so the server can re-check logins and later raise the costs.

Think of it like…

Salt is like adding a unique random spice to each customer's dish: even if two people order the same meal (password), the dishes taste different, so a thief cannot use one 'recipe book' of pre-cooked answers for everyone.

Real-world example

Orchid Books suffers a database breach. Because passwords were stored with Argon2id and a unique salt each, attackers can test only a handful of guesses per second per account on their hardware. Strong passwords survive, and the company has time to force resets before accounts are abused.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. When a user signs up, generate a random salt (e.g. 16 bytes).
  2. Run the password and salt through a slow password hash (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt).
  3. Store the salt, settings and resulting hash, never the password.
  4. At login, repeat the calculation with the stored salt and compare.
  5. For keys (not passwords), use a KDF like HKDF to derive separate keys from one secret.

Who uses it

Web and app developers, identity providers, operating systems, password managers, disk encryption and secure protocols.

Key takeaway

Store passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt/bcrypt) and a unique salt; never use plain MD5/SHA hashes or reversible encryption for passwords.

Going deeper

  • OWASP's minimum settings: Argon2id with 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations and 1 thread; scrypt N=2^17, r=8, p=1; bcrypt cost 10; or PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations.
  • Memory-hard functions force each guess to use lots of RAM, which is expensive on GPUs and custom chips; PBKDF2 is only CPU-hard and bcrypt uses about 4 KB, so attackers parallelise them more easily.
  • A pepper is an extra secret, kept in an HSM or configuration outside the database, mixed into every password hash so a stolen database alone is not enough to test guesses.
  • Hash strings such as $2b$12$..., $argon2id$... and $y$... record algorithm, cost and salt, letting systems upgrade old hashes transparently when users next sign in.
  • HKDF works in two steps: Extract concentrates entropy into a pseudorandom key using a salt, then Expand derives many labelled keys, so one secret safely feeds separate encryption and MAC keys.
  • NIST SP 800-63B requires salted, deliberately slow password hashing and advises checking new passwords against breached-password lists instead of forcing regular password changes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Encrypting passwords instead of hashing them; whoever holds the key can decrypt every password at once.
  • Using one global salt or the username as salt; salts must be random and unique for each password.
  • Feeding a human password into HKDF or a single SHA-256 pass to make a key; low-entropy passwords need slow password-based KDFs.
  • Setting cost parameters once and never revisiting them; raise them as hardware improves and rehash at next login.

docs.title: Try it: Derive a 32-byte key from a test password with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations)
docs.text: openssl kdf -keylen 32 -kdfopt digest:SHA256 -kdfopt pass:test-password -kdfopt salt:demo-salt -kdfopt iter:600000 PBKDF2

docs.title: Key algorithms, protocols & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example Argon2idBiryukov, Dinu & Khovratovich; RFC 9106 · Password hash · Recommended Winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition; tunable time and memory cost makes GPU cracking expensive. OWASP names Argon2id its first choice for storing passwords; Bitwarden and KeePassXC offer Argon2 to protect vault keys. bcryptProvos & Mazières (1999) · Password hash · Acceptable A battle-tested, adjustable-cost password hash based on Blowfish; only the first 72 bytes of a password count. Ruby on Rails, Laravel and many Node.js apps store user passwords as bcrypt hashes by default. scryptColin Percival; RFC 7914 · Password hash / KDF · Recommended A memory-hard function that forces attackers to spend lots of RAM per guess. Tarsnap backups and some cryptocurrency wallets protect keys derived from passphrases with scrypt. PBKDF2RSA Labs PKCS #5; RFC 8018; NIST SP 800-132 · Password-based KDF · Acceptable Repeats HMAC many times to slow guessing; FIPS-approved but not memory-hard, so needs high iteration counts. OWASP suggests about 600,000 iterations of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256; Wi-Fi WPA2 passphrases use PBKDF2. yescryptOpenwall (Alexander Peslyak) · Password hash · Recommended A scrypt-based password hash now used by default for Linux account passwords in many distributions. Debian 11+, Ubuntu 22.04+ and Fedora store login passwords in /etc/shadow as yescrypt ($y$) hashes. SHA-512cryptUlrich Drepper (glibc) · Password hash · Legacy A salted, iterated SHA-512 scheme; better than plain hashing but not memory-hard. Older Linux servers show '$6$' password hashes in /etc/shadow, made with SHA-512crypt. HKDFHugo Krawczyk; RFC 5869 · Key derivation function · Recommended Turns a shared secret into one or more strong keys; for high-entropy secrets, not passwords. TLS 1.3, Signal and HPKE derive their many session keys from one shared secret using HKDF. NIST SP 800-108 KDFsNIST · Key derivation functions · Recommended Standard counter, feedback and pipeline recipes for deriving keys from a master key using HMAC, CMAC or KMAC. Smart cards and HSMs derive per-session or per-device keys from a master key using SP 800-108 counter mode.

docs.title: 8.11 Random Number Generation
docs.text:
Every key, salt and nonce must be truly unpredictable, so cryptography depends on good random numbers. Computers gather "entropy" (unpredictable noise from hardware timing, electrical noise and so on) and feed it into a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSRNG) that produces endless unpredictable output.

From noise to keys on Linux. Applications should simply ask the operating system; all the mixing and reseeding happens underneath.

Think of it like…

It is like shuffling a deck of cards before a poker game: if the shuffle is predictable, everyone knows your hand no matter how good the table's lock is. Cloudflare even films a wall of about 100 lava lamps in its San Francisco lobby, and the unpredictable blobs feed extra randomness into its systems.

Real-world example

In 2008 a Debian code change accidentally removed most of OpenSSL's entropy, so only about 32,768 possible keys could be generated. Thousands of SSH and TLS keys made on Debian and Ubuntu systems were trivially guessable and had to be replaced. Good random number generation is invisible until it fails.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Hardware and the OS collect entropy from unpredictable events.
  2. The entropy seeds a cryptographic generator (DRBG).
  3. The generator produces as many random bytes as needed and is reseeded regularly.
  4. Applications ask the OS for randomness (getrandom, BCryptGenRandom) rather than inventing their own.
  5. HSMs and TPMs add hardware noise sources for high-assurance keys.

Who uses it

Operating systems, crypto libraries, HSM and chip makers, certificate authorities, game and lottery operators, and cloud providers.

Key takeaway

Always use the operating system's CSPRNG (or your crypto library's wrapper); never use rand(), Math.random() or timestamps for security.

Going deeper

  • Linux's random driver was overhauled in 2022: BLAKE2s now mixes entropy and a ChaCha20-based generator produces output, and since kernel 5.6 /dev/random no longer blocks once initially seeded.
  • NIST SP 800-90B defines how to test entropy sources and SP 800-90C how to build complete generators from them; FIPS 140-3 modules now need Entropy Source Validation certificates.
  • Virtual machines are risky: restoring a snapshot or cloning a VM can duplicate generator state, so hypervisors offer virtio-rng and a VM generation ID that triggers immediate reseeding.
  • A 2012 study ('Mining Your Ps and Qs') found many routers and embedded devices sharing RSA key factors because they generated keys at first boot with too little entropy.
  • Security needs unpredictability, not just statistical randomness: the Mersenne Twister passes statistical tests, yet its future output can be predicted after observing 624 outputs.
  • Randomness underpins everything: keys, nonces, IVs, salts, session IDs, ECDSA nonces and TLS handshake values, so one weak generator undermines all of them at once.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using Math.random(), rand() or Python's random module for tokens or keys; use crypto.getRandomValues, the secrets module or the OS generator.
  • Seeding a generator with the time or process ID, which attackers can guess within a small range.
  • Believing a blocking /dev/random is 'more secure'; on modern Linux, getrandom() and /dev/urandom are the correct choice.

docs.title: Try it: Generate 32 random bytes (e.g. for a test key) from OpenSSL's CSPRNG
docs.text:
openssl rand -hex 32
openssl rand -base64 24

docs.title: 8.12 Key Management & Secret Sharing
docs.text:
Strong algorithms are useless if keys are lost, stolen or never changed. Key management is the discipline of creating, storing, using, changing ("rotating") and finally destroying keys safely. Secret sharing splits one very important key into pieces held by different people, so no single person can use or lose it.

The key lifecycle. Every key should have a defined state and an owner at each stage, from creation to destruction.

Think of it like…

It is like a bank's safe-deposit system: a master key locks the box keys away, keys are swapped when staff leave, and the vault itself needs two managers turning their keys together.

Real-world example

Bluebell Hospital encrypts every patient file with its own data key, and those data keys are locked by a master key inside a hardware security module. Each year the master key is rotated without re-encrypting terabytes of files. The master key's backup is split with Shamir's scheme into five shares, any three of which can rebuild it, held by different directors.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Generate keys from a secure random source, ideally inside an HSM or cloud KMS.
  2. Build a hierarchy: master keys protect key-encryption keys, which protect the data keys.
  3. Give every key an owner, a purpose and an expiry date (cryptoperiod), then rotate it on schedule.
  4. Back up critical keys by splitting them into shares or escrowing them under strict control.
  5. When data or keys are retired, destroy the keys so the remaining ciphertext is unreadable.

Who uses it

Security architects, cloud and platform teams, certificate authorities, banks, HSM operators, crypto-custody firms and auditors.

Key takeaway

Never hard-code keys or store them next to the data they protect; use a KMS or HSM, rotate keys on a schedule and require more than one person for master keys.

Going deeper

  • NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 suggests cryptoperiods such as up to about two years for symmetric data-encryption keys and one to three years for private signing keys, adjusted for volume and risk.
  • Separate keys by purpose and environment: never encrypt and sign with the same key or share keys between test and production; derive purpose-bound keys with labelled HKDF calls.
  • In envelope encryption, rotation usually replaces the key-encryption key and re-wraps data keys, so terabytes of data need not be re-encrypted immediately.
  • Shamir's scheme hides the secret as the value at x=0 of a random polynomial of degree k-1; any k points rebuild it, while k-1 points reveal nothing at all.
  • PCI DSS requirement 3 sets key-management rules for card data, ISO/IEC 11770 defines key-management mechanisms, and auditors expect documented procedures plus a full key inventory.
  • Custody models range from provider-managed keys to customer-managed keys in a cloud KMS, BYOK and hold-your-own-key, trading convenience for control over who can decrypt.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Storing the encryption key in the same database or bucket as the encrypted data; one breach then exposes both.
  • Rotating keys but leaving old versions enabled for encryption forever; restrict retired keys to decryption and track which data still needs them.
  • Splitting a secret into shares but keeping all shares with one team or in one safe, which defeats the purpose.

docs.title: Try it: A two-level key hierarchy: a random data key encrypts a test file, then a master passphrase 'wraps' the data key
docs.text:
openssl rand -hex 32 > data.key
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in records.csv -out records.enc -pass file:data.key
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in data.key -out data.key.wrapped

A cloud database encrypts each table with its own DEK; only the KEK in the provider's KMS can unwrap them. A bank's new PKI uses RSA-3072 or P-256 so certificates issued now stay compliant beyond 2030. Shamir's Secret SharingAdi Shamir (1979) · Technique · Recommended Splits a secret into n shares so that any k of them rebuild it, while fewer than k reveal nothing at all. A company stores employees' BitLocker recovery keys in Microsoft Entra ID so help-desk staff can unlock a laptop after a failed update. A storage array and a database both obtain their encryption keys from the same KMIP key server.

docs.title: 8.13 Lightweight Cryptography for IoT
docs.text:
Tiny devices like sensors, smart cards, medical implants and RFID tags have very little memory, power and processing speed. Lightweight cryptography is designed to give strong protection while using a fraction of the energy and chip space of standard algorithms.

Lightweight cryptography milestones. After a decade-long search, NIST's choice of Ascon gave tiny devices a standard AEAD and hash.

Think of it like…

It is the difference between a bank vault door and a high-quality bike lock: the bike lock is light enough to carry everywhere yet still stops thieves.

Real-world example

GreenField Farms deploys battery-powered soil sensors that must last five years. The sensors encrypt and authenticate their readings with Ascon, which needs little code and energy. A neighbour with a radio receiver can hear the transmissions but cannot read or fake the moisture data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Assess the device's limits: memory, CPU, battery and radio budget.
  2. Pick an authenticated lightweight algorithm (Ascon) or hardware AES-CCM if present.
  3. Provision a unique key per device during manufacturing.
  4. Encrypt and authenticate every message, with a counter to block replays.
  5. Plan secure firmware updates so the crypto can be upgraded later.

Who uses it

IoT and embedded engineers, smart-meter, automotive and medical-device makers, RFID and smart-card vendors.

Key takeaway

Use Ascon or hardware-accelerated AES-CCM with unique per-device keys; avoid home-made or unvetted ciphers.

Going deeper

  • Constraints are measured in gate equivalents (chip area), RAM and ROM bytes, energy per bit and latency; lightweight designs save resources but must not drop below modern security levels.
  • Ascon is a sponge design built around a 320-bit permutation; one compact core provides authenticated encryption, hashing and extendable output, and it was designed with side-channel masking in mind.
  • Ascon-AEAD128 uses a 128-bit key, 128-bit nonce and 128-bit tag; as with every AEAD, a nonce must never repeat under the same key.
  • Many IoT radios, including Bluetooth LE and IEEE 802.15.4 chips, already contain AES hardware, so AES-CCM is often cheapest in practice; lightweight ciphers matter most where no such engine exists.
  • Key provisioning is often the hardest part: inject unique per-device keys or certificates at the factory, ideally into a secure element, rather than one shared key for a whole product line.
  • The EU Cyber Resilience Act and ETSI EN 303 645 require connected products to avoid universal default passwords, support secure updates and use appropriate, up-to-date cryptography.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using one shared network key across thousands of devices; extracting it from a single device compromises all of them.
  • Choosing a 64-bit-block cipher for high-volume data; small blocks hit collision limits quickly, so prefer Ascon or AES-CCM.
  • Forgetting replay protection; an attacker can resend an old valid 'unlock' command unless messages carry counters.

docs.title: 8.14 National & Regional Algorithm Suites
docs.text:
Governments publish lists of algorithms that their agencies, banks and suppliers must or should use. Some lists follow international standards (AES, SHA-2); others require home-grown national algorithms for reasons of sovereignty and trust.

Same job, different national rulebooks

United States China EU / Germany Block cipher AES SM4 AES Hash SHA-2, SHA-3 SM3 SHA-2, SHA-3 Signatures ECDSA, RSA, ML-DSA SM2 ECDSA (incl. Brainpool), RSA Certification FIPS 140-3 (CMVP) OSCCA commercial crypto Common Criteria (EUCC), BSI Post-quantum goal 2035 (CNSA 2.0, NIST) Own PQC standards under way High-risk systems by 2030

One product sold worldwide may need three sets of algorithms and certifications.

Think of it like…

It is like electrical plugs: the electricity is similar everywhere, but each country specifies its own socket, so products sold there must fit the local standard.

Real-world example

Meridian Payments wants to sell its card terminals in the US, China and Germany. For US federal customers it follows NIST FIPS 140-3 and NSA CNSA 2.0 guidance; for China it adds SM2, SM3 and SM4; for German public agencies it follows BSI TR-02102 and supports Brainpool curves. One product, three compliance checklists.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify which countries, sectors and customers you serve.
  2. Look up their required or recommended algorithm lists and deadlines.
  3. Design for crypto agility so algorithms can be swapped by configuration.
  4. Use certified libraries or modules (e.g. FIPS 140-3 validated) where required.
  5. Track post-quantum migration timelines set by each authority.

Who uses it

Government suppliers, defence contractors, banks, telecoms and multinational product vendors handling compliance.

Key takeaway

Build crypto agility into products so you can satisfy different national lists, and follow your regulator's post-quantum deadlines.

Going deeper

  • FIPS 140-3, aligned with ISO/IEC 19790, has four security levels; CMVP validation can take a year or more, so vendors list 'modules in process' publicly while they wait.
  • CNSA 2.0 stages its dates: quantum-resistant algorithms preferred from 2025 in signing and web software, exclusive use phased in between 2030 and 2033, and all national-security systems quantum-resistant by 2035.
  • China's Cryptography Law (in force since 2020) and GM/T standards require OSCCA-approved products in critical infrastructure; RFC 8998 defines TLS 1.3 cipher suites using SM2, SM3 and SM4.
  • Russian GOST algorithms are mandatory for certified government use, with GOST TLS cipher suites defined in RFC 9189 for TLS 1.2 and RFC 9367 for TLS 1.3.
  • Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) evaluates whole products; the EU's EUCC scheme, applicable since February 2025, is replacing national schemes and references agreed cryptographic mechanisms.
  • France's ANSSI and Germany's BSI publish their own rules (ANSSI's RGS guides, BSI TR-02102) and both recommend hybrid post-quantum key exchange during the transition.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating 'FIPS-compliant' and 'FIPS-validated' as the same; only modules holding a CMVP certificate are validated.
  • Hard-coding one country's algorithms into a product; other markets may require different suites, so design for crypto agility.
  • Assuming 'Regional' algorithms are weak; most are well studied and simply required or preferred in particular jurisdictions.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Data, Email, Governance & Specialized Security
docs.text: Attackers rarely want your computers for their own sake; they want the information and money behind them. This group covers tools that protect data directly, keep email and chat safe, stop fraud, prove to auditors and regulators that rules are followed, and secure special places like buildings, factories, smart devices, home life and AI systems. Think of it as protecting the treasure, the post, the paperwork and the unusual rooms of the building.

docs.title: 7.1 Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
docs.text:
Data Loss Prevention tools watch where sensitive information, such as card numbers, medical records or secret designs, is going. If someone tries to email it, upload it to a personal cloud drive or copy it to a USB stick, the tool can warn them, block it or alert the security team.

How a DLP policy decides. Context (who, where, which label) matters as much as what the content contains.

Think of it like…

It is like the security scanner at a museum exit: visitors can walk around freely, but nobody leaves carrying a painting under their coat.

Real-world example

At Brightwell Insurance, an employee tries to email a spreadsheet of 4,000 customer policy numbers to a personal Gmail address before starting a new job. The DLP policy recognises the pattern of policy and national insurance numbers and blocks the message. The employee sees a pop-up explaining why, and the security team gets an alert to follow up. No data leaves, and the company avoids a reportable breach.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define what counts as sensitive: card numbers, health data, source code, documents with a 'Confidential' label.
  2. Install DLP on endpoints, email, web gateways and cloud apps so it can see data moving.
  3. Write policies such as 'block uploads of customer data to personal storage'.
  4. Start in monitor-only mode, tune out false alarms, then switch to warn or block.
  5. Review alerts and coach staff; most incidents are mistakes, not malice.

Who uses it

Security and compliance teams in banks, healthcare, government, legal firms and any company handling personal or secret data.

Key takeaway

Start by watching, not blocking: a DLP tool that stops legitimate work on day one will be switched off by day two.

Going deeper

  • Detection techniques range from regular expressions validated by checksums (the Luhn check for card numbers) to exact data match against hashed database rows, document fingerprinting and trained ML classifiers for contracts or source code.
  • DLP covers three states: data in motion (email, web, network), data at rest (scans of file shares and cloud storage) and data in use (endpoint actions such as copy to USB, print, clipboard and screenshots).
  • Seeing HTTPS uploads requires TLS inspection at a proxy or Security Service Edge (SSE) cloud; endpoint agents see files before encryption, which is why most programmes combine network and endpoint DLP.
  • Modern DLP reads sensitivity labels stored in file metadata (for example Microsoft Purview labels), so policies can rely on a document's classification instead of re-scanning every byte.
  • Generative-AI DLP is the fastest-growing use case: SSE and browser-based tools inspect prompts and file uploads to chatbots and can block, redact or coach the user in real time.
  • Useful programme metrics include false-positive rate per policy, incidents per 1,000 users, mean time to triage and the share of policies running in block rather than monitor mode.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Switching on dozens of generic templates at once floods analysts with false positives; start with a few high-value data types and tune thresholds before adding more.
  • Assuming DLP stops a determined insider: phone photos of screens, encrypted archives and personal devices bypass it, so pair DLP with access control and insider-risk monitoring.
  • Ignoring employee-privacy law; content monitoring in the EU may need a legal basis, works-council consultation and clear notice to staff.

docs.title: 7.2 Data Security Posture Management & Data Discovery
docs.text:
Before you can protect data, you have to know where it is. These tools scan file shares, cloud storage, databases and SaaS apps to find sensitive information, label it, and show who can access it. Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) adds a running check of risky situations, such as a public cloud bucket full of customer records.

From unknown data to protected data. Discovery is only useful when findings end up with an owner and feed other controls.

Think of it like…

It is like a home inventory before insurance: you walk every room, list the valuables, and notice the jewellery box left by an open window.

Real-world example

Northgate Retail runs Cyera across its AWS and Microsoft 365 environments. Within a week it finds 37 forgotten database backups containing customer addresses, two of them readable by every employee. The team deletes old copies, locks down permissions and labels the rest as 'Restricted'. Their auditor later praises the clear data map.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Connect the tool to cloud accounts, file servers, databases and SaaS apps.
  2. It scans content and classifies data: personal, financial, health, secrets.
  3. It maps who and what can access each data store.
  4. It flags risks such as public exposure, excessive access or stale copies.
  5. Teams fix the issues and feed labels into DLP and encryption tools.

Who uses it

Data protection officers, cloud security teams and compliance staff in any data-rich organisation.

Key takeaway

Delete what you do not need: the safest sensitive data is the copy that no longer exists.

Going deeper

  • DSPM is mostly agentless: it uses cloud APIs and snapshot scanning, and many designs scan inside the customer's own account so raw data never leaves it. The category first appeared in Gartner's 2022 Hype Cycle for data security.
  • Classification usually samples objects instead of reading every byte, trading completeness for cost; tune sampling for very large buckets, data lakes and warehouses.
  • Shadow data such as forgotten backups, database snapshots, test copies and CSV exports is often the biggest finding; lineage tracking shows which production source each copy came from.
  • Access mapping links data to identities, roles and public links, where DSPM overlaps with CSPM and CIEM; many cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPPs) now bundle a DSPM module.
  • Outputs feed other controls: sensitivity labels for DLP and encryption, tickets for data owners, and the GDPR Article 30 record of processing kept by privacy teams.
  • On-premises tools such as Varonis add file-access auditing, so they can also detect abnormal activity like mass deletions or ransomware-style renames on file shares.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating discovery as a one-off project; data sprawl returns within months, so scan continuously and alert when new sensitive stores appear.
  • Trusting classifier labels blindly; check accuracy on samples, especially for non-English text and custom identifiers like policy or patient numbers.
  • Producing findings with no owner; give every data store a named business owner or remediation stalls indefinitely.

docs.title: 7.3 Privacy Management
docs.text:
Privacy laws such as the EU's GDPR and California's CCPA give people rights over their personal data. Privacy management tools help organisations ask for consent properly (for example, cookie banners), record what personal data they hold and why, and handle requests like 'show me my data' or 'delete my data' on time.

Handling a data subject request (GDPR). The one-month clock starts when the request arrives, not when it is verified by IT.

Think of it like…

It is like a well-run library's records desk: it knows which books (data) it holds about you, why, and can hand them over or remove them when you ask.

Real-world example

Fernleaf Travel receives about 300 data subject requests a month from customers across Europe. Using OneTrust, each request is verified, routed to the right systems and tracked against the one-month GDPR deadline. Their website consent banner, managed by the same platform, records exactly what each visitor agreed to. When the regulator asks questions, the team exports a complete audit trail.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map personal data: what is collected, where it is stored and why.
  2. Deploy a consent banner and preference centre on websites and apps.
  3. Set up a portal for access, correction and deletion requests.
  4. Run privacy impact assessments for new projects and vendors.
  5. Keep records and reports ready for regulators and auditors.

Who uses it

Privacy officers, legal teams, marketing and web teams in any business handling customer or employee data.

Key takeaway

A cookie banner must make 'Reject' as easy as 'Accept'; regulators actively fine sites that hide it.

Going deeper

  • GDPR gives one month to answer a data subject request, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests; California's CCPA/CPRA allows 45 days, extendable once by another 45.
  • GDPR Article 30 requires a record of processing activities (RoPA); privacy platforms build it from business questionnaires combined with automated data discovery.
  • Data protection impact assessments are mandatory under GDPR Article 35 for high-risk processing such as large-scale health data, profiling or systematic monitoring of public areas.
  • Consent management platforms block tags and cookies until consent, store a timestamped consent record and pass choices to ad partners through IAB TCF v2.2 or Google Consent Mode v2.
  • Global Privacy Control (GPC) is a browser signal that California and several other US states require businesses to honour as an opt-out of selling or sharing personal data.
  • More than 130 countries now have data protection laws, while the US relies on a patchwork of around 20 state privacy laws plus sector rules such as HIPAA and COPPA.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pre-ticked boxes, cookie walls and buried 'Reject' buttons do not give valid consent under EU rules; offer equally prominent Accept and Reject choices.
  • Deleting a person from the main database but forgetting logs, analytics, backups and vendors; map every copy and pass deletions downstream.
  • Weak identity checks on access requests turn the right of access into a data-leak route; verify requesters in proportion to the data's sensitivity.

docs.title: 7.4 Encryption Software for Files, Disks & Email
docs.text:
Encryption scrambles information so only someone with the right key can read it. Full-disk encryption protects everything on a laptop if it is lost or stolen; file encryption protects individual documents; email encryption protects messages in transit and in the recipient's inbox.

Three kinds of everyday encryption

Full-disk File / container Email Protects Whole drive when off Chosen files anywhere Message to recipient Examples BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS VeraCrypt, age, 7-Zip S/MIME, OpenPGP, Purview Key held by TPM / Secure Enclave + PIN Password or key file Recipient's private key Typical cipher AES-XTS AES-256 or ChaCha20 AES with RSA/ECC keys Does not cover Unlocked, running device Files left unencrypted Metadata, often subject

Each type protects a different situation, so most organisations need all three.

Think of it like…

It is like writing your diary in a secret code: anyone can steal the book, but without the codebook it is just gibberish.

Real-world example

A sales manager at Oakridge Medical leaves her laptop on a train. Because BitLocker was enabled with the recovery key stored in the company's Microsoft Entra ID, the thief sees only a locked screen and scrambled disk. IT confirms the device was encrypted, so the loss is not a reportable data breach. She gets a replacement laptop the next day.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Turn on full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS) on every laptop and phone.
  2. Store recovery keys centrally, not on a sticky note.
  3. Encrypt individual sensitive files or folders before sharing or uploading to the cloud.
  4. Use email encryption or sensitivity labels for confidential messages.
  5. Protect keys and passphrases: strong encryption with a weak password is weak.

Who uses it

Everyone with a laptop or phone, plus IT teams, healthcare, finance, lawyers and journalists.

Key takeaway

Full-disk encryption only protects a device that is switched off or locked, so always lock your screen.

Going deeper

  • BitLocker, FileVault and LUKS all use AES in XTS mode, designed for encrypting disk sectors; the volume key is sealed by the TPM or Apple's Secure Enclave and released only to an untampered boot chain.
  • TPM-only BitLocker unlocks automatically at boot; adding a pre-boot PIN defends against attacks that sniff the key from a discrete TPM's bus or exploit the running system before login.
  • LUKS2 uses Argon2id by default to slow passphrase guessing and has multiple key slots, so a user passphrase and a separate recovery key can both unlock the same disk.
  • OpenPGP (updated as RFC 9580 in 2024) and S/MIME are the two end-to-end email standards: S/MIME uses X.509 certificates built into Outlook and Apple Mail, OpenPGP uses user-managed keys.
  • age uses X25519 key agreement with ChaCha20-Poly1305, accepts SSH public keys as recipients and deliberately leaves out signing, keeping the tool small and hard to misuse.
  • Recovery-key escrow in Entra ID, Intune, Jamf or another MDM is what turns encryption into an enterprise control: IT can unlock devices and prove to regulators that a lost laptop was encrypted.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting old password-protected ZIP files: legacy ZipCrypto is weak; use AES-256 archives or age, with a long passphrase shared over a different channel.
  • Losing the recovery key means losing the data; escrow keys centrally and test a recovery before you actually need one.
  • Assuming disk encryption protects a running, logged-in laptop; malware and cloud sync see plaintext files, so endpoint security and file-level encryption are still needed.

age -r "$(age-keygen -y key.txt)" -o notes.txt.age notes.txt

docs.title: 7.5 DRM, Anti-Piracy & Document Rights Platforms
docs.text:
Digital Rights Management (DRM) keeps paid or confidential content under its owner's control. This section covers the services and vendors organisations actually buy: multi-DRM licence services for streaming, forensic watermarking and anti-piracy monitoring, and rights management that keeps business documents locked after sharing. The underlying technologies (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady, Common Encryption, HDCP) are explained in the "Content Protection & DRM" section of the cryptography chapters.

Multi-DRM playback with a licence service. The streaming company never runs key servers itself; the multi-DRM vendor issues a licence per device.

Think of it like…

It is like a library book that can only be read inside the library, with every copy secretly stamped with the borrower's name.

Real-world example

Lumen Studios releases a new series on its streaming service. Each episode is encrypted once and protected with Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady through a multi-DRM provider, so it plays on Android phones, iPhones, smart TVs and browsers. When a pirated copy appears online, an invisible forensic watermark identifies the subscriber account that leaked it. The account is closed and the copy is taken down.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Encrypt the content, often once using the Common Encryption standard.
  2. A licence server checks the viewer's subscription and device, then issues a key with rules such as expiry date or maximum resolution.
  3. Approved players decrypt inside protected hardware or software, so keys and video stay hidden.
  4. Add forensic watermarks to trace leaks back to a specific account or device.
  5. For business documents, apply rights such as 'view only' or 'expires in 30 days'.

Who uses it

Streaming services, film studios, broadcasters, publishers, game makers, and companies protecting confidential documents shared with partners.

Key takeaway

DRM raises the cost of copying but cannot stop someone filming a screen, so pair it with watermarking and fast takedowns.

Going deeper

  • Multi-DRM services hide Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady behind one API: the platform's backend signs an entitlement token, and the service checks it before issuing each device-specific licence.
  • Studio content-security requirements, such as MovieLabs' Enhanced Content Protection specification, expect hardware-backed DRM plus forensic watermarking for 4K and early-release films.
  • Streaming watermarks often use A/B variants: each video segment is prepared in two subtly different versions, and the CDN serves each viewer a unique sequence that spells out an ID.
  • Live sports piracy is fought in minutes: monitoring services find pirate restreams, read the watermark and revoke the leaking subscriber session while the match is still being played.
  • Enterprise rights management (Microsoft Purview, Seclore) encrypts the file itself and checks identity at every open, so control survives forwarding and USB copies; offline use relies on cached licences that expire.
  • Game anti-tamper such as Denuvo aims to protect the launch window, when most sales happen, and publishers often remove it months later once that period has passed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing DRM makes leaks impossible; screen capture and camcorder copies remain, so watermarking, monitoring and fast takedowns are essential.
  • Over-restricting paying customers with strict device limits or failing offline playback drives them towards pirate copies; balance protection with usability.
  • Leaving rights-management labels optional; a document shared without a label carries no protection once it leaves the company.

docs.title: 7.6 Backup & Ransomware Recovery
docs.text:
Backups are spare copies of your data that let you recover after accidents, hardware failure or ransomware (malware that locks files and demands payment). Modern backup tools make copies that attackers cannot change or delete. A good guide is the 3-2-1-1-0 rule: 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, 1 copy offsite, 1 copy offline or immutable (cannot be altered), and 0 errors when you test restoring.

Recovering cleanly from ransomware. Restoring the newest backup blindly can reinstall the attacker, so verify before you reconnect.

Think of it like…

It is like keeping photocopies of your passport: one in your bag, one at home, and one in a sealed envelope at a relative's house that nobody can scribble on.

Real-world example

Ransomware encrypts every server at Hollins Logistics on a Friday night. The attackers also deleted the backups they could reach, but the company's Veeam copies in immutable cloud storage could not be altered. Following its rehearsed recovery plan, the team restores critical systems by Sunday afternoon. They never pay the ransom.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what to back up and how much data loss and downtime is acceptable.
  2. Schedule automatic backups and follow the 3-2-1-1-0 rule.
  3. Make at least one copy immutable or air-gapped and protect backup admin accounts with MFA.
  4. Scan backups for malware and monitor for unusual mass changes.
  5. Test restores regularly; an untested backup is only a hope.

Who uses it

IT operations, security teams and every business or household with data they cannot afford to lose.

Key takeaway

Attackers hunt for backups first, so keep at least one copy they cannot delete, and practise restoring it.

Going deeper

  • The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured as time since the last good copy; the recovery time objective (RTO) is how long systems may be down.
  • Immutability is enforced by object lock (S3 Object Lock, Azure immutable blobs, B2 Object Lock), hardened Linux repositories or vendor appliances; S3 compliance mode cannot be shortened even by the account root user.
  • Attackers target backup consoles first, so keep backup admin accounts out of the main domain, require MFA and use multi-person approval for deletions, such as Veeam's four-eyes authorisation.
  • Backup platforms now detect ransomware from the data itself: spikes in change rate, high-entropy (encrypted-looking) files or mass extension renames flag suspicious restore points.
  • Large restores are limited by throughput: recovering 100 TB at 1 GB per second takes about 28 hours, which is why instant VM recovery and tiered recovery priorities matter.
  • SaaS follows shared responsibility: Microsoft, Google and Salesforce keep the service running but offer limited retention and recovery, so a separate backup of SaaS data is still needed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating sync, replication or RAID as backup; they faithfully copy deletions and encrypted files to every location.
  • Joining backup servers to the production domain with shared admin passwords; one stolen account can then destroy production and backups together.
  • Never testing full restores; many organisations discover missing systems, encryption keys or runbooks only in the middle of a real incident.
  • Restoring the newest backup without checking it; pick a verified clean point and close the original entry route first.

restic -r /mnt/backup/repo backup ~/Documents

docs.title: 7.7 Database Security & Activity Monitoring
docs.text:
Databases hold the crown jewels: customer records, payments and health data. Database security tools record who queries what, alert on suspicious activity such as an account suddenly downloading millions of rows, check databases for weak settings, and can block dangerous queries.

How database activity monitoring works. The monitor keeps its own tamper-resistant record, so even DBAs cannot erase their tracks.

Think of it like…

It is like a bank vault with a guard who writes down every person who enters, what they take out, and raises the alarm if someone fills a wheelbarrow.

Real-world example

At Crestview Credit Union, IBM Guardium notices a reporting account running a query that exports all 1.2 million member records at 3 a.m., something it has never done. An alert goes to the security team, who discover the account's password was stolen. They disable it and confirm from the logs exactly what was accessed. The detailed audit trail helps them meet regulatory reporting duties.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Discover all databases and find which contain sensitive data.
  2. Scan for weak settings, missing patches and default accounts.
  3. Monitor and log queries, especially from privileged users.
  4. Alert on or block unusual behaviour such as mass exports.
  5. Use logs for audits and incident investigations.

Who uses it

Database administrators, security teams and auditors in finance, healthcare, retail and government.

Key takeaway

Watch your administrators too: privileged accounts are the most valuable target for attackers.

Going deeper

  • Monitoring collects activity in three ways: host agents (which also see local privileged sessions), network capture (no database load but blind to local and encrypted traffic) and native audit logs such as pgAudit, Oracle Unified Auditing or SQL Server Audit.
  • Privileged users are a main reason DAM exists: an independent monitor whose logs the DBA cannot edit supports separation-of-duties requirements in PCI DSS, SOX and banking regulations.
  • Dynamic data masking hides values at query time, for example showing only the last four digits, while static masking permanently replaces data in test copies; both cut exposure outside production.
  • Encryption layers differ: transparent data encryption (TDE) protects files and backups at rest, column or application-level encryption hides fields even from DBAs, and TLS protects traffic.
  • Database firewalls learn the normal query shapes of each application and block anomalies, such as a UNION SELECT arriving from the web tier, as a backstop to secure coding.
  • Vulnerability assessment checks for default accounts, excessive grants, missing patches and internet exposure; CIS Benchmarks exist for Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Auditing every statement at full detail can slow busy databases and bury real signals; start with privileged users, sensitive tables and schema changes.
  • Believing TDE stops data theft; anyone querying through a stolen application account receives decrypted data, so access monitoring is still required.
  • Leaving unmasked production copies in development and test, where protection is weakest and breaches are common.

docs.title: 7.8 Email Security
docs.text:
Email is the most common way attacks start: phishing, malware attachments and fake invoices. Email security tools filter spam and malicious messages and check links and attachments. Three DNS records prove where mail really comes from: SPF lists the servers allowed to send for your domain, DKIM adds a digital signature showing the message was not altered, and DMARC tells receivers what to do (allow, quarantine or reject) when SPF or DKIM checks fail and sends you reports.

How a receiver checks SPF, DKIM and DMARC. DMARC passes only if SPF or DKIM passes and that domain matches the visible From address.

Think of it like…

SPF is the list of official post vans, DKIM is a tamper-proof wax seal on the letter, and DMARC is the instruction to the post office: 'If the seal is broken or the van is not ours, bin the letter and tell me.'

Real-world example

Criminals send emails pretending to be Lakeside Builders, asking suppliers to update bank details. Because Lakeside had set DMARC to 'reject' with help from dmarcian, most of the forged emails are rejected by recipients' mail servers. Meanwhile, Abnormal AI flags a real-looking message from a hacked supplier mailbox asking Lakeside to change payment details. The finance team calls the supplier and avoids losing 48,000 pounds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Route incoming mail through a secure email gateway or API-based protection.
  2. Scan attachments in a sandbox and rewrite links to check them when clicked.
  3. Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, then move DMARC from 'none' to 'reject'.
  4. Use AI tools to spot unusual requests like changed bank details.
  5. Give staff a 'report phishing' button and remove reported emails from all inboxes.

Who uses it

IT and security teams in every organisation, plus email administrators and domain owners.

Key takeaway

A DMARC policy of 'p=none' only watches; aim for 'p=reject' so others cannot send email pretending to be you.

Going deeper

  • DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes and the authenticated domain aligns with the visible From: header; this alignment is what stops forgers who pass SPF with their own domain.
  • SPF allows at most 10 DNS lookups per check; exceeding it causes a permanent error that can fail legitimate mail, so trim includes or move SaaS senders to subdomains.
  • Since 2024 Google and Yahoo require bulk senders (over 5,000 messages a day to Gmail) to use SPF, DKIM, DMARC of at least p=none, one-click unsubscribe and a spam rate under 0.3%; Microsoft added similar Outlook.com rules in 2025.
  • Secure email gateways sit in the MX path before delivery; API-based tools (integrated cloud email security) connect to Microsoft 365 or Gmail after delivery and can pull messages back. Many organisations layer both.
  • Business email compromise causes the largest reported losses: the FBI's IC3 recorded about 2.8 billion US dollars of BEC losses in 2024, far more than ransomware complaints.
  • Related standards: MTA-STS and TLS-RPT enforce encrypted delivery between mail servers, BIMI shows a verified logo for domains at DMARC enforcement, and ARC preserves results through forwarders and mailing lists.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving DMARC at p=none for years; it only reports. Use the reports to fix legitimate senders, then step through quarantine to reject.
  • Forgetting parked and non-sending domains; publish 'v=spf1 -all' and DMARC p=reject on them so they cannot be spoofed.
  • Assuming DMARC stops look-alike domains or hacked real mailboxes; those need AI-based detection, domain monitoring and call-back checks for payment changes.

docs.title: 7.9 Secure Messaging & Collaboration
docs.text:
Secure messaging apps use end-to-end encryption (E2EE), meaning only the sender and recipients can read messages, not the app company or anyone in between. Some also minimise metadata, such as who talked to whom and when. Encrypted email and meeting tools apply the same idea to mail and video calls.

End-to-end encryption, Signal style. The server stores only public keys and relays ciphertext; private keys never leave the phones.

Think of it like…

Normal messaging is like a postcard the postal service could read; end-to-end encryption is a locked box where only the recipient has the key.

Real-world example

Investigative reporter Maya at the Riverside Gazette talks to a whistleblower only through Signal, with disappearing messages set to one week. Even if the reporter's phone provider or Signal's servers were compelled to hand over data, they hold no readable messages. Documents are exchanged through Proton Mail to an editor's address, also encrypted. The source stays protected.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick an app that uses end-to-end encryption by default.
  2. Verify contacts' safety numbers or security codes for sensitive conversations.
  3. Turn on disappearing messages and app lock where helpful.
  4. Protect the device itself with a strong PIN and updates, since messages are readable there.
  5. For organisations, choose tools that meet retention and compliance rules.

Who uses it

Everyone, especially journalists, lawyers, activists, executives, healthcare staff and government officials.

Key takeaway

Encryption protects messages in transit, but a screenshot or an unlocked phone defeats it, so protect your devices too.

Going deeper

  • The Signal Protocol combines an initial key agreement (X3DH, upgraded to post-quantum PQXDH in 2023) with the Double Ratchet, giving each message a fresh key for forward secrecy and recovery after compromise.
  • Messaging Layer Security (MLS, RFC 9420, 2023) is the IETF standard for efficient end-to-end encryption in large groups; Wire adopted it and the GSMA's RCS Universal Profile 3.0 uses it for encrypted RCS.
  • Apple's PQ3 protocol (2024) added post-quantum key exchange and periodic rekeying to iMessage, so recorded traffic resists future quantum decryption.
  • Metadata still leaks: Signal's sealed sender hides who sent a message from its own servers, while many apps can still see who talks to whom, when and from which IP address.
  • Cloud backups are a weak spot: WhatsApp chat backups and iCloud data are end-to-end encrypted only if the user turns on encrypted backups or Advanced Data Protection.
  • Regulated firms must archive business messages; US regulators have fined financial firms well over 2 billion US dollars since 2021 for staff using unarchived personal messaging apps.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 'encrypted' means end-to-end; many chat and email services encrypt only in transit and on their servers, where the provider holds the keys.
  • Adding the wrong person to a group exposes every message to them; encryption cannot fix who you invite, so check group membership.
  • Ignoring safety-number change warnings; usually it is a new phone, but for sensitive contacts verify by call or in person.
