docs.title: 7.10 Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC) Platforms
docs.text:
Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) platforms are the organisation's central record of rules, risks and checks. They keep a list of risks and who owns them, the controls (safeguards) meant to manage them, policies, audits and evidence, replacing endless spreadsheets and email chains.

How GRC records link together. A failed control test automatically raises an issue and updates the risk it was meant to reduce.

Think of it like…

It is like a ship captain's logbook and checklist combined: every known hazard, every safety check, who did it and when.

Real-world example

Harbourview Bank must satisfy regulators, internal audit and its board. With ServiceNow IRM, each risk such as 'ransomware outage' is linked to controls like backups and MFA, each with an owner and regular tests. When a control test fails, a fix task is created automatically. The quarterly board report is now produced in an hour instead of two weeks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Build a risk register: list risks, rate their likelihood and impact, assign owners.
  2. Map controls to risks and to frameworks like ISO 27001 or NIST CSF.
  3. Schedule control tests and collect evidence.
  4. Track issues and fixes until they are closed.
  5. Report risk status to management, boards and regulators.

Who uses it

Risk managers, compliance officers, internal auditors and CISOs, especially in banking, insurance, healthcare and energy.

Key takeaway

A GRC tool is only as good as its data, so keep risk owners accountable for real updates, not tick-box entries.

Going deeper

  • Risk scoring usually multiplies likelihood by impact on a 5x5 matrix; mature teams add quantitative methods such as FAIR, expressing risk as expected annual loss in money.
  • The Institute of Internal Auditors' Three Lines Model: operations own risks, risk and compliance functions oversee, and internal audit gives independent assurance; GRC tools give each line its own views.
  • Key terms: inherent risk (before controls), residual risk (after controls), risk appetite and tolerance set by the board, and key risk indicators that trigger action when thresholds are crossed.
  • Common control libraries such as the Secure Controls Framework or Unified Compliance Framework provide ready mappings, so one control can satisfy many regulations at once.
  • Modern GRC integrates with vulnerability scanners, CMDBs and identity systems to test controls continuously, instead of sampling a handful of records once a year.
  • Broad suites covering enterprise, operational, IT, third-party and ESG risk are often marketed as integrated risk management (IRM).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Buying an enterprise GRC suite before agreeing processes; tools automate what exists, so define the risk method and ownership first.
  • Vague register entries like 'cyber attack'; write risks as cause, event and impact so controls can be linked and measured.
  • Colourful heat maps with false precision mislead boards; state assumptions and update scores with incident and metric data.

docs.title: 7.11 Security Frameworks, Standards & Regulations
docs.text:
Frameworks and standards are agreed rulebooks that describe what good security looks like; regulations are laws that make some of them compulsory, often with fines. Organisations pick the ones that apply to their industry, country and customers, then use GRC and compliance tools to prove they meet them. NIST CSF and the CIS Controls appear in the Security Operations chapter, and PCI DSS and cryptography standards in the cryptography chapters.

From law to evidence. One well-designed control set can satisfy several laws and standards at once.

Think of it like…

It is like building regulations: the code says how to build safely, the law says you must follow it, and the inspector's certificate proves you did.

Real-world example

Aldermoor Payments, a European fintech, maps its obligations: DORA because it is a financial firm, GDPR for customer data, and ISO 27001 because business customers ask for it. It builds one set of controls, such as MFA, backups and incident playbooks, and maps each to all three. When a key supplier suffers ransomware, the team already knows its DORA reporting deadlines and meets them. Its ISO 27001 auditor reuses the same evidence.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List the laws and contracts that apply, based on country, industry and customers.
  2. Choose a backbone framework, often ISO 27001 or NIST CSF.
  3. Map each requirement to shared controls so one safeguard satisfies several rules.
  4. Assign owners, collect evidence and run internal audits.
  5. Get certified or assessed where required, and track new rules and deadlines.

Who uses it

CISOs, compliance officers, risk managers, lawyers, auditors and boards in every regulated industry.

Key takeaway

Map once, comply many times: most frameworks ask for the same core safeguards, so build one control set and reuse its evidence.

Going deeper

  • ISO 27001:2022 has management-system clauses 4 to 10 plus Annex A's 93 controls in four themes; certificates run on a three-year cycle with yearly surveillance audits.
  • SOC 2 Type I tests control design at one point in time; Type II tests whether controls operated over a period, usually 3 to 12 months. Security is mandatory, while availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy are optional criteria.
  • Reporting clocks differ: NIS2 needs a 24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification and one-month final report; DORA an initial notice within 4 hours of classifying a major incident; GDPR 72 hours; the SEC four business days.
  • Maximum fines: GDPR up to 20 million euros or 4% of global turnover; NIS2 up to 10 million euros or 2% for essential entities; the EU AI Act up to 35 million euros or 7% for banned practices.
  • CMMC Level 1 covers 15 basic requirements, Level 2 the 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171, and Level 3 adds 24 requirements from NIST SP 800-172 assessed by the government.
  • Crosswalks such as NIST's OLIR mappings and the Secure Controls Framework show where ISO, NIST, SOC 2 and regulations overlap, enabling 'test once, comply many'.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing certification with full compliance: an ISO 27001 certificate covers only its stated scope, which may exclude key systems, so always read the scope statement.
  • Treating a SOC 2 report as a pass mark; it is an auditor's opinion with exceptions and excluded services that customers should actually read.
  • Assuming EU rules stop at the border; GDPR and the AI Act reach non-EU firms serving EU customers, and DORA and NIS2 duties flow to suppliers through contracts.

docs.title: 7.12 Compliance Automation
docs.text:
Compliance automation tools connect to your cloud, HR and code systems to check security controls continuously and gather audit evidence automatically, so getting certified takes weeks instead of months. Common frameworks: SOC 2 is a US audit report on how a service provider protects customer data; ISO 27001 is the international certification for an information security management system; GDPR is the EU law protecting personal data; HIPAA is the US law protecting patient health information; PCI DSS is the card industry's security standard for anyone handling payment cards.

Where compliance evidence comes from. Read-only integrations collect evidence continuously; failing tests become tasks for owners.

Think of it like…

It is like a fitness tracker for compliance: instead of guessing at your annual check-up, it measures every day and shows where you are slipping.

Real-world example

Pixelpath, a 40-person software startup, loses a big deal because it has no SOC 2 report. Using Vanta, it connects AWS, GitHub, Google Workspace and its HR system, and sees 60 failing checks, such as laptops without disk encryption. Over eight weeks the team fixes them, and the auditor pulls evidence directly from the platform. Pixelpath gets its SOC 2 report and wins the next deal.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a framework, such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001.
  2. Connect cloud, identity, HR, code and device management tools.
  3. Fix failing automated checks and adopt policy templates.
  4. Train staff and run required tasks such as access reviews.
  5. Share the evidence with an auditor and keep monitoring after certification.

Who uses it

Startups and growing SaaS companies, plus compliance and security teams that sell to enterprise customers.

Key takeaway

Passing an audit is not the same as being secure; use the framework as a floor, not a ceiling.

Going deeper

  • Platforms run hundreds of automated tests through read-only API connections, such as 'MFA enforced for all users', 'storage buckets encrypted' or 'leavers' accounts removed within one business day'.
  • Auditors still issue the result: the platform prepares evidence, but a licensed CPA firm signs a SOC 2 report and an accredited certification body issues ISO 27001 certificates.
  • Typical timelines: SOC 2 Type I readiness takes one to three months, while Type II needs an observation window of three to twelve months before the report can be issued.
  • Trust centres publish policies, certificates and NDA-protected reports to prospects, and AI features draft security-questionnaire answers from the evidence library.
  • Continuous control monitoring flags drift the day it occurs, closer to what regulators such as DORA expect than once-a-year point-in-time checks.
  • People controls that APIs cannot see, such as background checks, policy acceptance and training, are handled with built-in HR workflows and employee portals.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Adopting template policies unchanged; auditors test that you do what you wrote, so edit policies to match reality.
  • Connecting only part of the environment; legacy servers or unmanaged accounts outside the integrations surprise auditors and attackers alike.
  • Granting the platform broad write permissions; read-only roles limit damage if the compliance vendor itself is breached.

docs.title: 7.13 Third-Party & Vendor Risk / Security Ratings
docs.text:
Your suppliers can be your weakest link: many breaches start at a vendor with access to your data or systems. Vendor risk tools send and score security questionnaires and track contracts and evidence. Security ratings services look at a company from the outside (exposed systems, leaked credentials, patching) and give it a score, like a credit score for security.

The vendor risk lifecycle. Assessment depth follows the tier: critical vendors get the most scrutiny and monitoring.

Think of it like…

It is like checking a builder's reviews, licence and insurance before giving them the keys to your house.

Real-world example

Summit Health uses about 600 suppliers. With SecurityScorecard it watches their outside-facing security, and one billing vendor's score suddenly drops because of an unpatched VPN server. Summit's vendor manager contacts them, the vendor patches within 48 hours, and the evidence is recorded in their vendor risk platform. Later, when that vulnerability is widely exploited, Summit's data is safe.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List all vendors and rank them by how much data and access they have.
  2. Send security questionnaires (such as SIG or CAIQ) to important vendors and review evidence.
  3. Monitor vendors continuously with security ratings.
  4. Agree on fixes and contract terms such as breach notification times.
  5. Re-assess regularly and offboard vendors safely when contracts end.

Who uses it

Procurement, vendor management, security and compliance teams, especially in finance and healthcare.

Key takeaway

Outside-in ratings are a useful early warning, but always confirm with the vendor before drawing conclusions.

Going deeper

  • Tiering by data sensitivity, access and business criticality sets the depth of review: critical vendors get full questionnaires, SOC 2 Type II review and sometimes on-site audits; low-risk ones a short form.
  • Security ratings are built from outside-in signals: open ports, TLS and email settings, software versions visible in banners, malware infections seen by sinkholes, and leaked credentials.
  • Fourth parties (your vendors' suppliers) cause many incidents; the 2023 MOVEit Transfer breaches and the 2024 Change Healthcare attack showed how one shared provider can hit thousands of organisations.
  • Regulation now drives TPRM: DORA requires a register of all ICT third-party arrangements and exit strategies for critical services, and NIS2 explicitly covers supply-chain security.
  • Stronger evidence than self-attested questionnaires includes SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 certificates with scope, CSA STAR Level 2 attestations, pen-test summaries and software bills of materials.
  • Shared Assessments updates the SIG questionnaire every year, offering a Lite version for lower-risk suppliers and a full version for critical ones, both mapped to major frameworks.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Equating a completed questionnaire with assurance; self-attested answers need supporting evidence such as audit reports or certificates.
  • Treating a low rating as proof of poor security; ratings can misattribute IP addresses or shared hosting, so validate findings with the vendor.
  • Assessing only at onboarding; vendor risk changes, so monitor continuously and reassess critical suppliers at least yearly.

docs.title: 7.14 Configuration Hardening & Benchmarks
docs.text:
Hardening means switching off what you do not need and setting secure options, because systems usually ship with convenience-first defaults. Benchmarks are expert checklists of secure settings, and scanning tools compare your systems with them and show what to fix.

The hardening loop. Hardening is never finished: drift brings insecure settings back unless you keep scanning.

Think of it like…

It is like moving into a new house and changing the locks, closing unused doors and turning on the alarm before you unpack.

Real-world example

Greenfield County IT scans its Windows servers with CIS-CAT and scores only 54% against the CIS Benchmark: old protocols such as SMBv1 are enabled and guest accounts exist. Using Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit baselines as Group Policy, they fix most issues in a month. A re-scan shows 91%, and the remaining exceptions are documented with reasons. Their cyber insurance renewal goes smoothly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a benchmark for each system type (Windows, Linux, cloud, Kubernetes).
  2. Scan systems to measure current compliance.
  3. Test changes on a few machines, then roll out via Group Policy, Intune or Ansible.
  4. Document justified exceptions.
  5. Re-scan regularly to catch drift, the slow return of insecure settings.

Who uses it

System administrators, cloud engineers, security engineers and auditors, especially in government and regulated industries.

Key takeaway

Bake hardening into your base images and templates so every new system starts secure.

Going deeper

  • CIS Benchmarks offer Level 1 profiles (practical, low impact) and Level 2 profiles (defence in depth, may break features); DISA STIG findings are rated CAT I (high), CAT II and CAT III.
  • SCAP standardises machine-readable checks in XCCDF and OVAL formats, so OpenSCAP and DISA's SCAP Compliance Checker can run the same benchmark content and produce comparable reports.
  • Typical Windows first wins: disable SMBv1 and LLMNR, require SMB signing, remove local admin rights, deploy Windows LAPS for unique local passwords and turn on Credential Guard.
  • Golden images and infrastructure as code (Packer templates, CIS Hardened Images in cloud marketplaces) move hardening to build time, so every new server starts compliant.
  • Cloud accounts have their own benchmarks: CIS AWS, Azure and Google Cloud Foundations, checked continuously by posture tools such as AWS Security Hub and Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
  • Drift comes from manual fixes, new software and updates resetting options; desired-state tools such as Group Policy, Intune, PowerShell DSC and Ansible reapply settings on a schedule.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Applying a full Level 2 benchmark straight to production; some settings break applications, so test with pilot groups first.
  • Chasing a 100% score; aim for risk reduction and document accepted exceptions with an owner and review date.
  • Hardening once at build time and never rescanning; settings drift, so schedule regular scans and alerts.

docs.title: 7.15 Fraud Prevention & Transaction Monitoring
docs.text:
Fraud prevention tools check payments, logins and new account sign-ups in real time and score how likely each one is to be fraud. Banks use them to stop stolen cards, account takeovers and scams where victims are tricked into sending money; online shops use them to block fake orders without turning away genuine customers.

Real-time fraud decision. Most of the work happens in milliseconds, before the customer notices any delay.

Think of it like…

It is like an experienced cashier who notices when a customer's card, behaviour and shopping basket do not quite fit, and quietly calls the manager.

Real-world example

Late one evening, Juniper Bank's fraud system sees a customer log in from a new phone and try to send 9,500 pounds to a payee she has never used. Behavioural signals show she is typing hesitantly and switching between apps, as if someone is coaching her on a call. The payment is paused and the fraud team phones her, uncovering a fake 'bank security officer' scam. The money stays safe and the receiving account is reported.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Collect signals: device, location, typing behaviour, transaction history and shared fraud intelligence.
  2. Score each login, payment or order in milliseconds using rules and machine learning.
  3. Approve low-risk activity silently, add a check such as a one-time code for medium risk, and block high risk.
  4. Send suspicious cases to analysts, whose decisions are fed back to improve the models.
  5. Report confirmed fraud and suspected money laundering to authorities as the law requires.

Who uses it

Banks, card issuers, payment companies, online retailers, marketplaces, fintechs, gaming, travel and ticketing firms.

Key takeaway

Measure wrongly declined genuine customers as carefully as fraud losses, because both cost money and trust.

Going deeper

  • Decisions must be fast: a card authorisation typically completes in a fraction of a second end to end, so scoring models get tens of milliseconds to answer.
  • Signals include device fingerprints, IP reputation, impossible travel, behavioural biometrics, payee history, mule-account intelligence and consortium data shared between institutions.
  • Authorised push payment scams, where victims send money themselves, are now a top fraud type; since October 2024 UK payment firms must reimburse most victims up to 85,000 pounds, split between sending and receiving firms.
  • EU PSD2 strong customer authentication requires two independent factors for most online payments, with exemptions for low-value and low-risk transactions judged by transaction risk analysis.
  • EMV 3-D Secure 2 sends far richer device and transaction data than version 1, so issuers can approve most payments frictionlessly and challenge only risky ones; authenticated payments shift fraud liability to the issuer.
  • Anti-money-laundering monitoring is related but distinct: it looks for laundering patterns over weeks and leads to suspicious activity reports to the national financial intelligence unit.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Relying only on static rules; fraudsters probe and adapt within days, so combine rules with models that are retrained regularly.
  • Blocking too aggressively; false declines often cost merchants more than fraud itself and drive good customers to competitors.
  • Assuming one-time SMS codes stop scams; fraudsters coach victims to read out codes or approve payments themselves, so add behavioural and payee-risk checks.

docs.title: 7.16 Physical Security Systems: Access Control & Video Surveillance
docs.text:
Physical security systems protect buildings, rooms and people. Electronic access control lets people in with badges, phones or PINs and records every door opened, and video management systems (VMS) record and search CCTV cameras. These systems are now networked computers themselves, so they must be patched and protected like any other IT.

Electronic access control architecture. Every tier is a networked computer, so each needs patching, encryption and strong passwords.

Think of it like…

It is like a hotel where key cards open only the floors you are allowed on, and the front desk can see every corridor on its screens.

Real-world example

At Redwood Labs, a contractor's badge is used at the server room door at 2 a.m., an hour after his contract ended. The access control system denies entry and shows the clip from the nearest camera. The security officer sees a stranger holding the card and calls the police. Afterwards, HR and IT automate badge removal on each contract's end date.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Divide the site into zones and decide who may enter each one, and when.
  2. Install readers, door controllers and cameras, using encrypted credentials and the secure OSDP reader protocol.
  3. Link access control and video so every door alarm shows the matching footage.
  4. Remove access automatically when people leave, and review access rights regularly.
  5. Put cameras and controllers on their own network, change default passwords and keep firmware updated.

Who uses it

Corporate security and facilities teams in offices, data centres, hospitals, schools, airports, retail and critical infrastructure.

Key takeaway

Old 125 kHz proximity badges can be copied in seconds, so move to encrypted smart cards or mobile credentials.

Going deeper

  • Card choice matters: 125 kHz proximity cards have no cryptography, MIFARE Classic's Crypto1 cipher is broken, while MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3 and HID SEOS use AES and are today's recommended options.
  • Wiegand, the legacy reader wiring, sends card numbers in clear; OSDP 2.2 with Secure Channel adds AES-128 encryption and line supervision and is standardised internationally as IEC 60839-11-5.
  • Mobile credentials in Apple Wallet and Google Wallet use the phone's secure element over NFC, can work without unlocking in express mode, and are harder to clone than plastic cards.
  • Video systems interoperate through ONVIF profiles; cloud video needs strong admin MFA, as the 2021 Verkada breach showed when a leaked super-admin credential exposed around 150,000 cameras.
  • Physical identity and access management (PIAM) links badges to HR and identity systems, so joiner, mover and leaver events grant or revoke door access automatically.
  • Tailgating defeats valid badges, so high-security areas add turnstiles, mantraps, anti-passback rules or video analytics that count people per badge swipe.
  • CCTV is personal data under GDPR: sites need signage, a defined purpose, limited retention (often 30 days or less) and a process for footage access requests.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving cameras and recorders on the office network with default passwords; they become botnet members or entry points, so segment and patch them.
  • Badge-only entry to high-security rooms; add a PIN or biometric and anti-passback to stop shared or cloned cards.
  • Slow access removal; tie badges to HR leaver processes so contractors lose access on their last day.

docs.title: 7.17 OT / ICS / Industrial Security
docs.text:
Operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) run physical things: power grids, water plants, factories and pipelines. They often use old equipment that cannot be patched or rebooted easily, so OT security tools mostly listen quietly to network traffic to inventory devices, spot threats and suggest safe fixes without disrupting production.

The Purdue model for industrial networks. Traffic between IT and OT should pass through the industrial DMZ, never straight down to controllers.

Think of it like…

It is like a doctor monitoring a patient in intensive care: you watch every vital sign closely, but you cannot just switch the patient off and on to fix something.

Real-world example

Bluewater Utilities runs Dragos sensors in its water treatment plant. The platform builds a full inventory of 1,400 controllers and alerts when an engineering laptop starts sending commands to change chemical dosing settings at midnight. Operators confirm it is not authorised, isolate the laptop and keep the plant running safely. The investigation reveals a compromised remote access account.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Passively map all OT assets and how they communicate.
  2. Separate OT from office networks using zones and firewalls (as in ISA/IEC 62443).
  3. Monitor industrial protocols for unusual commands and known threat behaviour.
  4. Prioritise vulnerabilities by real risk, since many devices cannot be patched quickly.
  5. Plan incident response together with engineers and safety teams.

Who uses it

Utilities, manufacturing, oil and gas, transport, pharmaceuticals, hospitals' building systems and government infrastructure teams.

Key takeaway

In OT, safety and uptime come first; use passive monitoring and never run aggressive scans on live controllers.

Going deeper

  • Industrial protocols such as Modbus/TCP, DNP3, S7comm and EtherNet/IP were designed without authentication, so anyone on the network can send commands; secure variants like OPC UA security and CIP Security exist but adoption is slow.
  • ISA/IEC 62443 organises plants into zones and conduits with target security levels SL 1 to 4; part 3-3 sets system requirements and part 4-2 sets requirements for individual components.
  • Landmark incidents: Stuxnet (2010) sabotaged centrifuges, attacks on Ukraine's grid (2015, 2016) cut power, TRITON (2017) targeted safety systems, and Colonial Pipeline (2021) halted operations after IT ransomware.
  • Passive monitoring copies traffic from switch SPAN ports or taps to build an asset inventory; optional active queries use native protocol reads at low rates and only with engineers' approval.
  • Remote access is a top entry route: use dedicated secure remote access gateways with MFA, session recording and time-limited vendor approval instead of always-on VPNs or remote-desktop tools.
  • Patches may wait months for planned outages, so compensating controls such as segmentation, application allow-listing and monitoring carry the load; CISA's ICS advisories help prioritise.
  • Sector rules apply: NERC CIP standards are mandatory for the North American bulk electric grid, and NIS2 covers energy, water, transport and manufacturing operators in the EU.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pointing ordinary IT vulnerability scanners at PLCs; aggressive scans have crashed controllers and stopped production, so use passive or vendor-approved methods.
  • Believing the plant is air-gapped; most sites have remote access, shared historians or vendor laptops bridging IT and OT.
  • Leaving OT incident response to IT alone; engineers and safety staff must decide when and how to isolate or shut down safely.

docs.title: 7.18 IoT & Connected Device Security
docs.text:
The Internet of Things (IoT) means everyday devices that connect to networks: cameras, printers, smart TVs, medical pumps and door locks. They often cannot run security software, so specialised tools identify each device by its network behaviour, flag risky ones and limit what they can talk to. Standards and certifications help buyers choose safer devices.

Why IoT needs different security

Laptop IoT / medical device Security agent EDR installed Usually impossible Patching Monthly, automatic Vendor-dependent, often never Identity User login, certificate MAC address, maybe certificate Lifespan 3-5 years 10-15+ years Visibility Agent telemetry Network traffic only Main control Endpoint protection Segmentation and NAC

Most IoT devices cannot run an agent, so the network has to do the protecting.

Think of it like…

It is like a building manager who knows every delivery person by sight and only lets each one into the rooms they actually need.

Real-world example

Maple Grove Hospital uses Ordr and discovers 9,000 connected devices, including 300 infusion pumps on old software. The tool places the pumps in their own network segment where they can only talk to the drug library server. Months later, malware spreads through an office PC, but it cannot reach the pumps. Patient care continues as normal.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Discover every connected device and identify its type, maker and software.
  2. Assess risks: default passwords, old firmware, known vulnerabilities.
  3. Segment devices so each can only talk to what it needs.
  4. Monitor for unusual behaviour, like a camera contacting foreign servers.
  5. Buy certified or well-supported devices and change default passwords.

Who uses it

Hospitals, retailers, universities, smart buildings, manufacturers and households with smart home gadgets.

Key takeaway

Put smart devices on a separate network (or guest Wi-Fi at home) so a hacked camera cannot reach your laptop.

Going deeper

  • Agentless identification combines MAC vendor prefixes, DHCP and mDNS fingerprints, protocol behaviour and passive traffic analysis, matched against large libraries of known device profiles.
  • Enforcement usually reuses existing infrastructure: network access control (802.1X or MAC authentication bypass), VLANs, firewall policies or switch ACLs pushed by the visibility platform.
  • NIST IR 8259A defines six baseline capabilities for IoT makers: device identification, device configuration, data protection, logical access to interfaces, software update and cybersecurity state awareness.
  • Laws now set minimums: the UK PSTI regime bans universal default passwords, the EU Cyber Resilience Act covers connected products, and the US Cyber Trust Mark labels consumer devices.
  • Medical devices live for decades and need regulatory approval for changes; since 2023 the US FDA requires cybersecurity plans and software bills of materials for new connected devices.
  • The 2016 Mirai botnet hijacked cameras and routers with default passwords and launched huge DDoS attacks, including one on DNS provider Dyn that disrupted major websites.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Relying on MAC filtering; MAC addresses are trivial to spoof, so combine identification with behaviour monitoring and certificates where possible.
  • Buying devices without checking their support period; ask how many years of security updates are guaranteed before purchase.
  • Flat networks where cameras can reach servers; segment by function and allow only the flows each device needs.

docs.title: 7.19 Personal & Consumer Security
docs.text:
Security is not just for companies. A few free tools protect individuals from most everyday threats: a password manager for unique passwords (compared in the Identity chapter), alerts when your data leaks, privacy-friendly browsers and ad blockers, credit freezes against identity theft, and special high-security modes for people at higher risk.

Personal security in priority order. The first three steps stop most account takeovers that ordinary people suffer.

Think of it like…

It is like home safety basics: good locks, a smoke alarm and a spare key with a trusted neighbour stop most problems before they start.

Real-world example

Retired teacher Ruth gets an email from Have I Been Pwned saying her address appeared in a data breach at a shopping site. She had reused that password for email, so she switches to Bitwarden, creates unique passwords and turns on two-step verification. She also freezes her credit with the three US credit bureaus. A month later, someone tries to open a credit card in her name and is refused.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Use a password manager and give every account a unique password or passkey.
  2. Turn on two-step verification, starting with email and banking.
  3. Subscribe to breach alerts and run your platform's security checkup.
  4. Keep devices and browsers updated and use a content blocker.
  5. Freeze your credit, and turn on high-security modes if you are at higher risk.

Who uses it

Everyone: families, students, seniors, freelancers, and higher-risk people like journalists and activists.

Key takeaway

Your email account is the master key to everything else, so give it a unique password and strong two-step verification first.

Going deeper

  • Passkeys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) resist phishing because the device only releases a login to the genuine website; Apple, Google, Microsoft and many banks and shops now support them.
  • SMS codes beat no second factor but are exposed to SIM-swap fraud; authenticator apps or passkeys are stronger, and a mobile carrier account PIN or port-out lock adds protection.
  • Have I Been Pwned lists more than 14 billion breached accounts, and its Pwned Passwords service lets apps check passwords anonymously using a k-anonymity range search.
  • US credit freezes at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion have been free by law since 2018; the UK has no equivalent freeze, but Cifas Protective Registration flags your name for extra checks.
  • Protective DNS services such as Quad9, and content blockers in browsers, stop known-malicious domains and malvertising for every device on a home network.
  • Stalkerware and controlling partners are a real threat at home; Apple Safety Check and Google's Security Checkup show who can see your location, accounts and devices.
  • People at high risk, such as journalists and activists, can add Google's Advanced Protection Program, Android Advanced Protection or Apple Lockdown Mode (covered in the Endpoint chapter).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reusing one password across sites; a single breach unlocks many accounts through credential stuffing, so use unique passwords from a manager.
  • Expecting a VPN to make you anonymous or phishing-proof; it only hides traffic from the local network and internet provider.
  • Reading out one-time codes or approving prompts during unexpected calls; real banks and support desks never ask for them.

docs.title: 7.20 AI for Security & Security for AI
docs.text:
This covers two sides. AI for security means assistants that help defenders work faster, for example summarising alerts or writing investigation queries in plain English. Security for AI means protecting AI systems such as chatbots from attacks like prompt injection (hidden instructions that trick the AI), data leaks and harmful outputs, through testing tools and guardrails.

Guardrails around an AI application. No single filter is enough; limiting what the model can access and do is the strongest control.

Think of it like…

AI for security is giving the security guard a brilliant assistant; security for AI is making sure that assistant cannot be sweet-talked by a stranger into opening the vault.

Real-world example

Quill Bank launches a customer-service chatbot. Before launch, its red team uses PyRIT and Garak to test thousands of tricky prompts and finds the bot can be tricked into revealing internal policy notes. They add Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields and tighten the bot's access, then retest. Meanwhile, the SOC uses Microsoft Security Copilot to summarise incidents, cutting triage time per alert from 20 minutes to 5.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Use AI assistants in the SOC to summarise, investigate and draft reports, with humans checking results.
  2. Inventory your own AI apps and the data and tools they can access.
  3. Test AI apps against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications with red-teaming tools.
  4. Add guardrails that filter prompts and outputs, and limit what the AI is allowed to do.
  5. Monitor AI usage, log interactions and retest after every model or prompt change.

Who uses it

SOC analysts, AI and ML engineers, application security teams, risk managers and any company building or using AI.

Key takeaway

Treat everything an AI reads (emails, web pages, documents) as untrusted, and never give it more access than the user it serves.

Going deeper

  • Prompt injection tops the 2025 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (LLM01); indirect injection hides instructions in web pages, emails or documents the model reads, so filters alone cannot fully solve it.
  • Agentic AI raises the stakes: when models can call tools, send email or run code, use least privilege, require human approval for risky actions and keep untrusted content apart from instructions.
  • The model supply chain needs checking: downloaded models and datasets can carry malicious pickle code or backdoors, so prefer the safetensors format, scan artefacts and keep an AI bill of materials.
  • Red-teaming combines automated scanners (Garak, PyRIT, Promptfoo) with human testers; findings are mapped to OWASP and MITRE ATLAS and rerun as regression tests after every model or prompt change.
  • Governance is maturing: EU AI Act obligations for general-purpose AI models applied from August 2025, with high-risk system rules phasing in later; ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF provide management structure.
  • Shadow AI, staff pasting company data into unapproved chatbots, is handled with approved enterprise AI tools that do not train on customer data, DLP or SSE controls and a clear usage policy.
  • SOC assistants speed up summaries and query writing, but analysts must verify their output, and the AI's own actions should be logged for audit.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Relying on the system prompt to keep secrets or rules; assume anything in the prompt or context window can be extracted by a user.
  • Treating guardrail products as complete protection; they reduce but never eliminate jailbreaks, so restrict what the AI can reach and do.
  • Accepting AI-generated investigation conclusions unchecked; models can invent hosts, indicators or query results that do not exist.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Endpoint & Device Security
docs.text: An 'endpoint' is any device people actually use: laptops, desktops, phones, tablets and servers. Because attackers usually break in through one of these devices, protecting them is one of the most important jobs in security. This group covers the tools that stop malware, keep devices updated and configured, control what can run, manage devices remotely, protect servers and virtual desktops, and record what happens so problems can be spotted and fixed fast.

docs.title: 3.1 Endpoint Detection & Response / XDR
docs.text:
Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) software watches everything happening on a computer, such as programs starting, files changing and network connections, and raises an alarm when behaviour looks like an attack. It also lets security staff respond remotely, for example by cutting an infected laptop off the network. XDR (Extended Detection and Response) goes further by joining signals from computers, email, cloud accounts and the network into one picture.

From sensor event to contained laptop. Good EDR closes the loop: one detection becomes a block on every device.

Think of it like…

Classic antivirus is a bouncer checking IDs at the door; EDR is a security team with CCTV in every room that notices when a 'guest' starts picking locks and can lock that room instantly.

Real-world example

At Northfield Logistics, an accountant opens a fake invoice that quietly launches PowerShell and tries to dump stored passwords. The company's EDR spots this unusual chain of events within seconds and automatically isolates the laptop from the network. The security analyst sees a timeline showing exactly which file started it, removes the malware remotely, and blocks the same file on all 2,000 other devices. The attacker never reaches the payroll servers.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A small software 'sensor' is installed on every laptop, desktop and server.
  2. The sensor records activity (processes, files, logins, network connections) and sends it to a central console, usually in the cloud.
  3. Detection rules, behaviour analysis and machine learning flag suspicious patterns such as ransomware-like file encryption.
  4. Analysts or automated playbooks respond: isolate the device, kill the process, delete the file, or roll back changes.
  5. XDR adds email, identity, cloud and network data so one attack can be followed across all systems.

Who uses it

Security operations centre (SOC) analysts, IT security teams and managed security providers in almost every mid-size and large organisation.

Key takeaway

An EDR is only as good as the people or service watching its alerts, so pair it with a 24/7 team or a managed detection and response (MDR) service.

Going deeper

  • Sensors collect process starts with full command lines, parent-child chains, file writes, registry changes, network connections and logons; on Windows they use kernel callbacks, ETW and file-system minifilter drivers.
  • XDR correlates endpoint data with email, identity, cloud and network telemetry. 'Native' XDR relies on one vendor's stack; 'open' XDR ingests third-party tools through connectors.
  • Standard response actions include network isolation (keeping only the console connection), killing processes, quarantining files, collecting a forensic package, remote shell scripts and fleet-wide hash blocking.
  • MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations and labs such as AV-Comparatives and SE Labs measure detection visibility and protection; results show capability, not how well a product fits your team.
  • The July 2024 CrowdStrike content-update failure crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, prompting staged content rollouts and Microsoft's push to run security tools outside the kernel.
  • Key SOC measures are mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR) and sensor coverage, because every device without a healthy sensor is a blind spot.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving EDR in detect-only mode for months; once tuned, enable prevention and automatic isolation or alerts arrive after the damage.
  • Assuming full coverage while Linux servers, contractor laptops and new cloud VMs lack sensors; reconcile EDR inventory against asset lists every month.
  • Adding broad folder exclusions for performance gives attackers a safe hiding place; keep exclusions narrow, documented and regularly reviewed.
  • Leaving tamper protection off lets intruders uninstall or blind the agent; enable it and alert whenever a sensor goes silent.

docs.title: 3.2 Antivirus & Endpoint Protection
docs.text:
Antivirus software scans files, downloads and running programs to find and block malicious software (malware) such as viruses, ransomware and spyware. Modern products do more than match known 'fingerprints': they also watch behaviour, check web links and use cloud lookups to catch brand-new threats. Endpoint Protection Platforms (EPP) are the business versions, managed centrally for many devices.

How modern antivirus catches malware. Each layer catches what the one above misses; signatures alone stop only known files.

Think of it like…

It is like a flu vaccine plus a thermometer: it recognises known illnesses immediately and also notices when you start running a fever from something new.

Real-world example

Priya, a freelance designer, downloads a 'free font pack' that actually contains a password-stealing program. Microsoft Defender Antivirus on her laptop recognises the file's behaviour from cloud data, quarantines it before it runs, and shows a notification. She deletes the download and changes nothing else, because nothing was stolen.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The product installs on the device and keeps a constantly updated list of threat signatures and behaviour rules.
  2. Real-time protection scans files as they are downloaded, opened or run.
  3. Suspicious files are checked against cloud reputation services and behaviour monitoring.
  4. Threats are blocked, quarantined (locked away) or removed, and the user or admin is alerted.
  5. Scheduled scans sweep the whole device for anything that slipped through.

Who uses it

Everyone: home users, small businesses and large organisations, usually as the baseline layer under EDR.

Key takeaway

Run exactly one real-time antivirus at a time, keep it updated automatically, and never switch it off to make something 'work'.

Going deeper

  • Detection combines signatures for known files, heuristics and machine-learning models for unknown files, cloud reputation lookups, and behaviour monitoring of what a program actually does after starting.
  • Windows' Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) lets antivirus inspect PowerShell, VBScript, JavaScript and Office macros after de-obfuscation, catching fileless script attacks that never touch disk as normal files.
  • AV-TEST, AV-Comparatives and SE Labs test protection, false positives and performance several times a year; prefer products that score consistently across many rounds rather than one headline result.
  • Microsoft Defender Antivirus switches to passive mode when another antivirus is registered, and 'EDR in block mode' lets Defender for Endpoint remediate threats the third-party product misses.
  • The EICAR test file is a harmless, industry-standard text string every antivirus detects, used to confirm real-time protection and alerting work without handling real malware.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running two real-time antivirus engines together causes slowdowns and conflicts; use one, plus an on-demand second-opinion scanner if needed.
  • Believing antivirus alone stops modern attacks; intruders use legitimate tools such as PowerShell, so pair it with EDR, patching and MFA.
  • Excluding whole folders to fix a slow application; exclude specific files or processes only after testing, and review exclusions regularly.

docs.title: 3.3 Mobile Device & Unified Endpoint Management
docs.text:
Mobile Device Management (MDM) lets an organisation set up, secure and control phones, tablets and laptops from one central place. Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) is the same idea covering every kind of device: Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android and more. Admins can push apps and settings, require passcodes and encryption, and wipe a lost device remotely.

Zero-touch enrolment of a company iPad. Access to email is granted only after the device proves it is compliant.

Think of it like…

It is like a school handing out lockers with a master key: every locker follows the same rules, and the office can open or clear any locker if needed.

Real-world example

Coastline Health gives 800 nurses iPads. Using Microsoft Intune, IT ships the boxes straight to the wards; when a nurse signs in, the iPad automatically installs the patient-records app, enforces a six-digit passcode and turns on encryption. When one iPad is left on a bus, IT wipes the work data remotely within minutes, and the hospital avoids a data breach report.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Devices are enrolled, ideally automatically through Apple Business Manager, Android Zero-Touch or Windows Autopilot.
  2. Admins define policies: passcode rules, encryption, Wi-Fi, VPN, allowed apps and update schedules.
  3. The MDM pushes settings and apps to devices over the internet.
  4. Compliance checks report devices that are out of date or rule-breaking, and access to email or apps can be blocked until fixed.
  5. Lost, stolen or departing-employee devices can be locked, located or wiped remotely.

Who uses it

IT administrators in companies, schools, hospitals and governments that hand out or allow work devices, including personal phones (BYOD).

Key takeaway

Enrol devices automatically from the start, and for personal phones manage only the work apps and data so employees' privacy is respected.

Going deeper

  • Apple MDM wakes devices through the Apple Push Notification service (APNs); the device then checks in with the MDM server, so the push certificate must be renewed every year with the same Apple ID.
  • Supervised iPhones and iPads, enrolled through Automated Device Enrollment, allow stronger controls such as non-removable management profiles, app restrictions and single-app kiosk mode.
  • Android Enterprise offers fully managed mode for company phones and a work profile for personal phones, keeping work apps and data in a separate container IT can wipe.
  • Compliance policies covering OS version, encryption, passcode, jailbreak or root, and threat risk feed identity providers such as Entra ID Conditional Access, so non-compliant devices lose access automatically.
  • Apple's Declarative Device Management, introduced in 2022, lets devices apply and report settings autonomously, and Apple is moving software-update enforcement from older MDM commands to it.
  • For BYOD, Intune app protection policies (MAM) can encrypt and restrict corporate data inside Outlook or Teams without enrolling the personal phone at all.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Managing personal phones as fully managed devices invades privacy and drives refusals; use work profiles or app protection policies for BYOD.
  • Letting the yearly Apple push certificate expire, or renewing it with a different Apple ID, breaks management of every Apple device.
  • Sending a full wipe when a selective wipe of work data was intended; document and test which wipe type each scenario uses.

docs.title: 3.4 Mobile Threat Defense & App Vetting
docs.text:
Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) apps protect phones and tablets from risky apps, phishing links, dangerous Wi-Fi networks and outdated or tampered operating systems. App vetting means checking an app for malware, privacy leaks or weak security before people install it, either by app store reviewers or by security testing tools. Together they help keep the small computer in everyone's pocket safe.

How MTD risk blocks company data. MTD detects; the MDM and identity provider enforce.

Think of it like…

MTD is like a smoke detector for your phone, while app vetting is the food inspector who checks a restaurant before it is allowed to open.

Real-world example

A sales rep at Brightwave Media gets a text claiming a parcel is waiting, with a link to a fake delivery site. Lookout on her company phone blocks the page as phishing before she can enter anything. Meanwhile, the company's developers scan their own new app with MobSF before release and discover that it stored login tokens in plain text, which they fix before launch.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An MTD app is installed on the phone, often pushed automatically by the MDM.
  2. It checks installed apps, the OS version, device settings and network connections for risks.
  3. It blocks phishing links in texts, emails and messaging apps.
  4. Risk scores are shared with the MDM so a risky phone can lose access to company data until fixed.
  5. App vetting tools analyse app files (APK/IPA) for malware, insecure storage, hidden trackers and weak encryption.

Who uses it

Mobile security teams, MDM administrators, app developers and penetration testers, especially in finance, healthcare and government.

Key takeaway

Most phone attacks start with a link, so pair MTD phishing protection with keeping the phone's OS updated.

Going deeper

  • MTD watches four risk areas: the device (OS version, jailbreak or root), apps (malicious or leaky), networks (rogue Wi-Fi, TLS interception) and content (phishing links in SMS, email and chat).
  • On iOS, apps cannot inspect other apps, so MTD phishing protection usually works through a local VPN or DNS filter; Android allows deeper scanning of installed apps.
  • Mercenary spyware such as NSO Group's Pegasus has used zero-click exploits; Apple sends threat notifications to targeted users, and Lockdown Mode shrinks the attack surface for high-risk people.
  • App vetting combines static analysis (decompiling APK or IPA files for hard-coded secrets, permissions and insecure storage) with dynamic analysis of live traffic, guided by OWASP MASVS and MASTG.
  • SMS phishing ('smishing') and QR-code phishing ('quishing') bypass email gateways entirely, which is why link protection on the phone itself matters.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming iPhones need no protection; phishing, malicious configuration profiles and outdated iOS versions are real risks without traditional malware.
  • Blocking every medium-risk device on day one floods the help desk; start in report mode, then enforce high-risk blocking.
  • Treating app-store review as a guarantee; risky and data-hungry apps still slip through, so vet business-critical apps yourself.

docs.title: 3.5 Patch & Software Update Management
docs.text:
A 'patch' is an update that fixes a bug or security hole in software. Patch management tools find which devices are missing updates and install them on a schedule, so known weaknesses are closed before attackers use them. Many major breaches came from flaws that already had a fix available but were never installed.

The monthly patch cycle. Rings let a small pilot catch bad updates before everyone gets them.

Think of it like…

It is like a car recall service that tracks every car in a fleet and books each one in for the free repair before the faulty part fails.

Real-world example

Maple Street Credit Union's IT team of three looks after 450 Windows PCs and 30 servers. Using Windows Autopatch for PCs and an Automox policy for servers and third-party apps such as Chrome and Zoom, updates roll out first to a small test group, then to everyone a few days later. When an emergency browser fix is released, they push it to all devices within 24 hours and confirm 98% compliance on the dashboard.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Scan all devices to build an inventory of operating systems, apps and missing updates.
  2. Rank missing patches by risk, putting actively exploited flaws first.
  3. Test updates on a small pilot group of devices.
  4. Roll out in waves on a schedule, with restarts planned outside working hours.
  5. Report compliance and chase devices that failed or were offline.

Who uses it

IT operations and desktop support teams, server administrators and managed service providers in every sector.

Key takeaway

Patch internet-facing systems and actively exploited vulnerabilities (such as those on CISA's KEV list) first, within days rather than weeks.

Going deeper

  • Microsoft releases security updates on Patch Tuesday, the second Tuesday of each month, and ships out-of-band fixes when a flaw is already being exploited.
  • Under CISA Binding Operational Directive 22-01, US federal agencies must fix KEV-listed vulnerabilities by set due dates, typically two weeks for newly added recent CVEs.
  • The Australian Essential Eight expects patches for internet-facing services within 48 hours when a working exploit exists, and within two weeks otherwise.
  • Third-party apps such as browsers, PDF readers, Java and meeting clients are often more exposed than the OS; catalogues like Patch My PC or ManageEngine package them automatically.
  • Linux distributions publish advisories (Ubuntu USN, Red Hat RHSA, Debian DSA); live patching fixes the running kernel, but updated user-space services still need restarting.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reporting 'patches deployed' instead of 'devices updated and rebooted'; measure installed state, including laptops that were offline.
  • Forgetting firmware, VPN gateways and network appliances; many mass-exploited flaws sit in edge devices outside the normal patch tool.
  • Testing forever or not at all; a pilot ring of a few days catches most bad monthly updates.

docs.title: 3.6 Remote Monitoring & Management (RMM) & Remote Support
docs.text:
Remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools let IT teams and IT service providers look after many computers from one web console: checking health, installing updates, running scripts and taking over the screen to help a user. Because one RMM login can reach every device, these tools are powerful for defenders and a prize for attackers, who also trick people into installing remote-support apps. Securing RMM means locking down who can use it and blocking any remote tool you did not approve.

One RMM console reaches everything. Because the hub controls every device, it needs the strongest protection of all.

Think of it like…

An RMM is like a master key ring for every office in a building: hugely convenient for the caretaker, but if it is copied or stolen every door opens, so it needs a strong safe and a sign-out log.

Real-world example

Bluewater IT Services looks after 45 small businesses using NinjaOne. After reading about criminals abusing remote-access tools, it requires phishing-resistant MFA for every technician, limits who can run scripts on all clients at once, and records every remote session. It also uses application control to block remote apps it does not use. When a scammer phones a client's receptionist pretending to be IT support and asks her to install AnyDesk, the app refuses to run and Bluewater gets an alert.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose one approved RMM and remote-support tool and install its agent on every managed device.
  2. Protect the console with phishing-resistant MFA, role-based permissions and alerts for unusual logins.
  3. Use it to monitor device health, push patches and scripts, and give remote help with the user's consent and a session log.
  4. Patch the RMM product itself quickly, especially self-hosted servers, because attackers target known flaws in these tools.
  5. Block or alert on any unapproved remote-access software using application control and EDR.

Who uses it

Internal IT and help desks, managed service providers (MSPs) who run IT for small businesses, and security teams who audit remote access.

Key takeaway

Treat your RMM console like a top-level administrator account: phishing-resistant MFA, least privilege, audit logs, and an alert whenever an unknown remote-access tool appears.

Going deeper

  • RMM agents run as SYSTEM or root on every managed machine, so the console is effectively administrator access to all customers; protect it like a privileged access management tool.
  • The 2021 Kaseya VSA attack reached about 60 managed service providers and up to 1,500 downstream businesses; CVE-2024-1709 in ScreenConnect allowed authentication bypass and was mass-exploited.
  • CISA advisory AA23-025A (2023) warned that criminals abuse legitimate remote tools because they are signed and trusted, often after phone or email 'help desk' scams.
  • Good practice: SSO with phishing-resistant MFA, per-client role separation, approval for mass script runs, session recording, and forwarding RMM audit logs to the SIEM.
  • Self-hosted RMM keeps data in-house but makes you responsible for patching an internet-facing server quickly; cloud RMM shifts that duty to the vendor.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Allowing many remote tools because someone once used them; standardise on one or two and block the rest with application control.
  • Shared technician logins hide who did what; give each technician a named account with MFA and least privilege.
  • Leaving unattended access permanently enabled on every device; restrict it to devices and hours that truly need it.

docs.title: 3.7 Application Control, Allowlisting & Least Privilege
docs.text:
Application control decides which programs are allowed to run on a device. With 'allowlisting', only approved software can run and everything else is blocked by default, which stops most malware and ransomware even if it has never been seen before. Endpoint privilege management adds 'least privilege': people work without full administrator rights, and only approved tasks are given extra rights.

Blocklisting vs allowlisting

Blocklist (antivirus) Allowlist (app control) Default Run unless known bad Block unless approved New malware May run until detected Blocked automatically Setup effort Low Higher: audit, rules, requests Best fit General-purpose PCs Servers, kiosks, OT, admin PCs Example tools Defender AV, ESET App Control, ThreatLocker, Santa

Allowlisting flips the default, so brand-new malware is blocked without a signature.

Think of it like…

Instead of keeping a list of known troublemakers to turn away, it is a guest list at a private party: if your name is not on it, you do not get in.

Real-world example

Riverbend Water Authority runs the computers that control its treatment plant. Using ThreatLocker allowlisting, only the plant software, Windows and a few approved tools can run. When an engineer plugs in a USB stick carrying ransomware, the malicious program simply refuses to start because it is not on the approved list, and the security team receives an alert showing the blocked file.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run the tool in 'audit' (learning) mode to record which software is genuinely used.
  2. Build rules that approve software by publisher signature, file hash or trusted folder.
  3. Switch to 'enforce' mode so unapproved programs and scripts are blocked.
  4. Give users a simple way to request new software, with approvals by IT.
  5. Review blocked events regularly and update rules as software changes.

Who uses it

Security teams in critical infrastructure, healthcare, finance and government, and organisations following frameworks such as the Australian Essential Eight.

Key takeaway

Start in audit mode and allow by trusted publisher signature where possible, so updates do not break things.

Going deeper

  • Rules approve software by publisher (code-signing certificate), file hash or path. Publisher rules survive updates, hash rules are strictest, and path rules are weakest wherever users can write files.
  • Windows App Control policies can also block known-vulnerable drivers; Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist is on by default in Windows 11 2022 Update and later, stopping 'bring your own vulnerable driver' attacks.
  • Application control is the first of the Australian Signals Directorate's Essential Eight strategies and maps to CIS Control 2, which asks organisations to inventory and allowlist authorised software.
  • When App Control or AppLocker is enforced, PowerShell runs untrusted scripts in Constrained Language Mode, which limits the advanced features attackers rely on.
  • Removing local administrator rights is high impact: most malware needs elevation, and standard users cannot disable security tools or install unapproved software.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Allowing folders users can write to, such as Downloads or AppData, lets malware simply run from there; allow by signer instead.
  • Jumping straight to enforce mode breaks business apps; run audit mode for several weeks and review the logs first.
  • Trusting everything Microsoft-signed; attackers abuse built-in tools like mshta.exe, so add deny rules for unneeded 'living-off-the-land' binaries.

docs.title: 3.8 Browser & Web Isolation Security
docs.text:
The web browser is where people spend most of their working day, so it is a favourite target for phishing, malicious downloads and data theft. Browser security tools manage browser settings and extensions centrally, block dangerous sites and stop sensitive data being copied out. 'Remote browser isolation' opens websites on a remote server and streams only a safe picture to your screen, so harmful code never reaches your computer.

Remote browser isolation in action. Risky code runs in the cloud; only a safe rendering reaches the laptop.

Think of it like…

Browser isolation is like handling a suspicious package with robot arms behind glass: you can see and use it, but it can never touch you.

Real-world example

Harbor Insurance lets claims staff use Chrome Enterprise with policies that block unknown extensions and warn on risky downloads. Links in emails from outside the company open through Menlo Security's isolation service. When an employee clicks a link to a booby-trapped website, the malicious code runs harmlessly in the cloud and the laptop stays clean.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. IT manages browsers centrally, pushing security settings, approved extensions and update rules.
  2. Safe-browsing and web-filtering services warn about or block known phishing and malware sites.
  3. Risky or unknown sites can be opened in an isolated remote browser instead of locally.
  4. Enterprise browsers add data controls such as blocking copy-paste, printing or uploads of sensitive data.
  5. Browser activity and threats are reported to the security team.

Who uses it

IT and security teams, especially in organisations with remote staff, contractors on unmanaged devices, or strict data-protection needs.

Key takeaway

Keep browsers auto-updating and control which extensions are allowed, because a malicious extension can see everything you do online.

Going deeper

  • Browsers are managed through policies: Group Policy or Intune for Edge and Chrome, Chrome Enterprise Core in the cloud, and policies.json or ADMX templates for Firefox.
  • Malicious extensions are a major risk: in December 2024 attackers phished developer accounts and pushed poisoned updates to dozens of Chrome extensions, including Cyberhaven's.
  • Chrome's Manifest V3 extension platform limits content-blocking rules, which is why Chrome users moved to uBlock Origin Lite while Firefox still runs full uBlock Origin.
  • Isolation comes in two styles: pixel streaming, where only images reach the device, and DOM reconstruction, where a cleaned page is rebuilt locally; they trade security against speed and compatibility.
  • Infostealer malware steals session cookies to bypass MFA; Chrome's App-Bound Encryption (2024) and device-bound session credentials aim to make stolen cookies much harder to reuse.
  • Enterprise browsers enforce copy, print and upload controls on unmanaged contractor devices without VDI, a fast-growing alternative for third-party access.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Letting users install any extension; allowlist approved ones and scrutinise permissions like 'read and change all your data on all websites'.
  • Isolating every website slows users and breeds workarounds; isolate risky categories such as uncategorised, newly registered and emailed links.
  • Leaving browser password saving on unmanaged profiles hands credentials to infostealers; use a managed password manager instead.

docs.title: 3.9 Virtual Desktops & Secure Workspaces (VDI / DaaS)
docs.text:
With a virtual desktop, the user's Windows desktop and apps actually run on a server in a data centre or the cloud, and only a picture of the screen travels to their device. VDI (virtual desktop infrastructure) is the self-hosted version; DaaS (desktop as a service) is rented from a cloud provider. Because company data never sits on the laptop, a lost, shared or personal device exposes far less.

Where a virtual desktop really runs. Only screen pixels and input cross the gateway; data stays in the back end.

Think of it like…

It is like studying a museum's treasures through a live video link: you can see every detail, but the treasures never leave the vault.

Real-world example

Lakeside Bank hires 150 contractors who work from their own laptops. Instead of shipping them company PCs, it gives them Azure Virtual Desktop sessions with copy-paste, file downloads and local printing switched off, plus MFA at sign-in. When one contractor's laptop is infected with password-stealing malware, the attacker finds no bank data on it, and the security team simply resets the account and reviews the session logs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. IT builds a hardened 'golden image' of Windows with approved apps, security agents and settings.
  2. Users connect through a gateway with single sign-on and MFA, from a laptop, thin client or web browser.
  3. Policies control clipboard, drive mapping, printing, USB and screenshots, and can add on-screen watermarks.
  4. Non-persistent desktops reset to the clean image at log-off, wiping anything picked up during the session.
  5. Gateways, hosts and images are patched and monitored like any other critical server.

Who uses it

IT teams in banking, healthcare, government and call centres, and any organisation with contractors, offshore teams or staff using personal devices.

Key takeaway

Require MFA and patch internet-facing gateways urgently, because one stolen password or unpatched gateway (as in the 'Citrix Bleed' NetScaler attacks) exposes every desktop behind it.

Going deeper

  • Display protocols include Citrix HDX (ICA), Microsoft RDP, Omnissa Blast Extreme and HP Anyware's PCoIP; each encrypts the session and sends only screen updates and input.
  • Non-persistent pooled desktops reset at log-off while persistent desktops keep changes; profile containers such as FSLogix carry user settings across non-persistent sessions.
  • Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, available through Azure Virtual Desktop, lets several users share one virtual machine, cutting cost compared with one VM per person.
  • Gateways are prime targets: 'Citrix Bleed' (CVE-2023-4966) leaked NetScaler session tokens so attackers hijacked sessions despite MFA, and 'CitrixBleed 2' (CVE-2025-5777) followed in 2025.
  • VDI does not make the endpoint irrelevant: keyloggers and screen-capture malware on the user's own device can still see what is typed and displayed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming VDI keeps data inside while clipboard, drive mapping and printing redirection stay open; restrict them by policy.
  • Neglecting golden-image patching re-deploys old vulnerabilities to every desktop at each refresh; patch and rebuild images monthly.
  • Publishing RDP directly to the internet instead of through a gateway with MFA invites brute-force and exploit attacks.

docs.title: 3.10 Host Telemetry & Visibility
docs.text:
Host telemetry tools record detailed information about what is happening on computers and servers: which programs started, who logged in, which files changed, which network connections were made. This 'flight recorder' data is sent to a central place so security teams can detect attacks and investigate incidents. Many of these tools are free and open source.

Key telemetry sources by operating system

Windows Linux macOS Built-in source Event Log + ETW auditd, journald Unified Log + ESF Rich process data Sysmon Sysmon for Linux, eBPF ESF-based agents Logons Events 4624 / 4625 auth.log / secure Unified Log Query state osquery osquery osquery Forwarding WEF or agent rsyslog or agent Agent via MDM

Built-in logs give the basics; add a rich sensor and a query tool on every platform.

Think of it like…

It is like a building's visitor log and CCTV combined: most days nobody looks, but after an incident it shows exactly who went where and when.

Real-world example

After a suspicious alert, the security team at Pinecrest University wants to know whether an attacker's tool exists anywhere else. Using live osquery queries through Fleet, they search all 3,000 university machines for the file in under ten minutes and find it on two more servers. Sysmon logs on those servers show the exact command that downloaded it, helping them clean up and close the hole.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install a lightweight agent or enable built-in logging (such as Sysmon or auditd) on each device.
  2. Configure what to record, for example process launches, logins, file changes and network connections.
  3. Forward the data to a central SIEM, log store or console.
  4. Write detections and dashboards, and run queries to hunt for threats across all devices.
  5. During incidents, collect deeper evidence (memory, files, artefacts) from affected machines.

Who uses it

Security analysts, threat hunters, incident responders, and IT/compliance teams who need device inventory and audit trails.

Key takeaway

Use a tested starting configuration (for example a community Sysmon config) to capture useful events without drowning in noise.

Going deeper

  • Windows Security event IDs worth memorising: 4624 successful logon, 4625 failed logon, 4688 process creation, 4720 user created, 4732 member added to a local group, 1102 audit log cleared.
  • Sysmon event IDs: 1 process creation with hashes and command line, 3 network connection, 11 file created, 13 registry value set, and 22 DNS query.
  • Command-line capture for event 4688 must be switched on by Group Policy, and PowerShell Script Block Logging (event 4104) records de-obfuscated script content, one of the most valuable Windows logs.
  • On Linux, eBPF lets tools such as Falco, Tetragon and modern EDR sensors observe system calls safely inside the kernel without loading risky kernel modules.
  • osquery exposes hundreds of tables, such as processes, listening_ports and chrome_extensions, so the same SQL question works across Windows, macOS and Linux.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting every event verbatim floods the SIEM and budget; start from a tuned config such as SwiftOnSecurity's or sysmon-modular.
  • Keeping logs only on the device; attackers clear them (event 1102), so forward logs off-host within seconds.
  • Ignoring clock synchronisation; unsynchronised hosts make incident timelines unreliable, so enforce NTP everywhere.

docs.title: 3.11 Server & Linux Host Protection
docs.text:
Servers run websites, databases and business systems, often on Linux, and need protection suited to them: nobody sits at the keyboard and they must stay running. Server protection combines limiting what each program is allowed to do, spotting unexpected changes to important files, and applying security fixes, sometimes without even restarting. Hardening checklists (CIS, STIG) are covered in the Governance chapter and network blockers such as Fail2ban in the Network chapter.

Defence in depth on a Linux server. If an attacker beats one layer, the next one limits or reveals them.

Think of it like…

It is like securing a bank vault rather than a shop: few people go in, everything has a fixed place, and anything that moves unexpectedly is investigated.

Real-world example

Greenleaf Online runs its web shop on 40 Ubuntu servers. AppArmor profiles stop the web server touching anything outside its own folders, AIDE checks system files every night, and Canonical Livepatch applies kernel fixes without reboots. When attackers exploit a plugin flaw, AppArmor blocks their attempt to read sensitive files, and the next AIDE check flags the file they dropped, which the team removes the same morning.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from a minimal, hardened server build and remove services and software that are not needed.
  2. Turn on mandatory access control (SELinux or AppArmor) so each program can only touch what it needs.
  3. Install a server protection or EDR agent plus file-integrity monitoring to catch malware and unexpected changes.
  4. Apply security updates automatically, using live patching for the kernel where reboots are difficult.
  5. Send logs and alerts to the security team and investigate them like any other incident.

Who uses it

System administrators, DevOps and site reliability engineers, hosting providers and security teams running on-premises or cloud servers.

Key takeaway

Never switch SELinux or AppArmor off to 'make an app work'; fix the policy instead, because they often stop attacks that get past everything else.

Going deeper

  • SELinux labels every file and process with a security context and enforces type-enforcement rules; modes are enforcing, permissive (log only) and disabled.
  • AppArmor confines programs with path-based profiles in enforce or complain mode; Ubuntu ships profiles for many common services and confines Snap packages by default.
  • PCI DSS v4.0 requirement 11.5.2 requires a change-detection mechanism such as file integrity monitoring to alert on unauthorised changes to critical files.
  • eBPF-based enforcement in Tetragon can kill a process the instant it breaks policy, rather than only alerting afterwards as traditional log-based tools do.
  • Live patching replaces vulnerable kernel functions in memory; it covers critical security fixes, but servers still need periodic reboots into fully updated kernels.
  • SSH hardening basics: key-based authentication, no direct root login, password authentication disabled, and AllowUsers or AllowGroups restricting who may connect.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running 'setenforce 0' to make an application work; fix labels, booleans or policy with audit2allow instead of disabling protection.
  • Running file integrity monitoring without a baseline-update process, so every patch triggers alerts; tie baseline updates to change management.
  • Assuming cloud servers are secured by the provider; under shared responsibility the operating system and applications remain yours.
